title: feat(029): supply-chain provenance: signed images, SBOM attestation, air-gap bundles
body:
## Summary

Spec 029 section 3: every published image is signed and describable, and there is an offline install path.

- **Signing (3.1).** cosign keyless over the Actions OIDC identity signs both the per-arch images and the multi-arch manifest list. The manifest signature is the one that matters: `cosign verify ghcr.io/statecrafting/enrahitu:latest` checks the list, because that is what a tag pull resolves to.
- **SBOM (3.2).** An SPDX SBOM is generated with syft and attached as a cosign attestation. Four things enter the image with no package manifest naming them (rauthy, the Encore runtime, and both SPA bundles), so they are injected explicitly. Verified against a real image: syft catalogues 301 packages and none of the four is among them.
- **rauthy pinned by digest (3.4).** Replaces the mutable `0.36.0` tag. This is the OCI index digest, not a leaf manifest, so `--platform` still resolves the right leaf and the multi-arch build of spec 016 is unaffected. Pinning a leaf would have silently broken the other architecture.
- **Air-gap bundle (3.3).** `scripts/airgap-bundle.sh` produces the offline path: the image archive, its signature material, a checksum manifest over every member, a generated `verify.sh`, and the operator manual for exactly the version inside. One bundle per architecture, because `docker load` on a stock daemon cannot consume a multi-platform archive.
- **Triggers (spec 016 amendment).** `image.yml` now runs on push to main, building and smoking both arches without publishing or signing, because nothing else built the image on main and main carried image breakage silently twice. Section 5 of spec 016 excluded this on a premise about two long Rust builds that spec 018 deleted; the measured run is 80 seconds. Publishing stays off push, so the actual exclusion in section 5 is preserved.

Three spec premises were corrected in the spec before coding rather than coded around: a multi-arch `docker save` archive is not loadable by a stock daemon (so bundles are per-arch), the tsparser is not in the image at all (so an SBOM entry for it would be a false statement of contents), and the syft catalogue contains none of the four items above.

## Testing

- `npm test` (462 tests), `npm run typecheck`, `spec-spine compile`, `lint --fail-on-warn`, `index check`, `check:chassis`, `check:infra`, `check:manifest`, `check:licenses`, and actionlint: all clean.
- Twelve tests in `scripts/airgap-bundle.test.ts` cover the verifier, each mutation-checked. They found a real defect: `sha256sum` on Darwin reports an absent file only on stderr and prints no FAILED line on stdout, so the first verifier passed a bundle with a member deleted, which made removing the SBOM or the verifier itself undetectable. Members are now checked for existence by looking, not by reading the output of the tool.
- Proven end to end locally: the bundle was built from a real `docker save`, the local tag was deleted, the image was loaded only from the bundle, and it ran under `--network none`. First boot provisioned, `/healthz`, `/readyz` and `/hiq/health` answered 200 within six seconds, the SPA served, OIDC discovery served with the right issuer, and the login endpoint returned its 302 into the IdP. Driving a browser through to a session is the harness of spec 017 and was not done.

Three acceptance items cannot be closed from a working tree: no tag has been signed, so no `cosign verify` has ever succeeded; the attestation round trip is unexercised; and no release assets exist. Spec 029 therefore stays `implementation: in-progress` with a dated status note naming exactly what is open.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: chassis.lock (owned by spec 035) changes here with no authoring edit to 035. The diff is mechanical only: five regenerated hashes for files this change edits, plus two roster entries for the new scripts/airgap-bundle.sh and its test. No chassis boundary rule and no upgrade semantic changes, so editing 035 would be ratifying a regenerated artifact rather than recording a design decision.

title: fix(034,037,028): the precondition each caller had to remember
body:
## Summary

A freshly provisioned cell has no control-plane schema, because migration is a deploy step and never a boot step (spec 032 §3.6). Every controller started anyway, read `controller_watermark` on its first pass, threw `no such table`, logged it, slept a tick, and repeated. The out-of-box state of a new cell was a permanent 1 Hz error loop, until an operator ran `migrate --apply`. Recorded as a defect for spec 034 in spec 028 amendment item 4; this closes it.

**What was wrong was the altitude of the check, not its absence.** Spec 036 §3.6 already required this behavior and `backend/members/boot.ts` already implemented it. The mail runtime, arriving later, did not, because nothing in `startController` required its caller to have thought about it. A precondition each caller must remember is one each new caller eventually forgets, and the second one already had.

The wait therefore moves into the loop that holds the precondition:

- `startController` waits for the control-plane tables before its first pass. It says so once and then says nothing. A controller written tomorrow inherits this.
- The waiter is cancellable, so `stop()` does not have to outlast a poll interval.
- The mail sweep takes the same gate. It is not a controller: it scans `resource` on its own minute timer, so it held its own copy of the defect, quieter and equally permanent.
- A failing probe keeps waiting and reports on a distinct log line. Propagating one would turn a transient into a permanently dead controller: worse than the noise it replaces, and silent.

**`runOnce` needed its guarantee written down.** It got its single pass from the loop synchronous prefix, before `startController` returned. Awaiting the schema yields first, so the guarantee evaporated and three existing spec 034 tests failed. The loop is now a `do`/`while`, and the behavior no longer depends on scheduling.

`docs/OPERATIONS.md` stops describing the error loop as the expected state of a new cell. The troubleshooting entry keeps one sentence about the old log line, because a cell running an older image still produces it.

## Testing

- Full suite: 450 passed, 12 skipped, 36 files. `npm run typecheck` clean.
- `spec-spine compile` / `lint --fail-on-warn` (0/0/0) / `index check` fresh. `check:model` fresh, `check:licenses` clean, `check:chassis` fresh.
- New `backend/control/schema-gate.test.ts` runs against a node whose migration has never been applied, the only state in which the property is visible.
- **The assertion is on the log, because the log is the defect.** A first draft asserted that no reconcile ran and the watermark stayed at 0, and it passed against the unfixed code: the old loop threw at `readWatermark`, several statements before anything a reconciler would see, so both were true while it failed forty times a second.
- Every half mutation-checked: bypassing the controller gate fails with 35 recorded pass failures, removing either `cancel()` hangs the relevant tests at 20s, and bypassing the sweep gate fails its assertion.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: chassis.lock is spec 035 owned artifact and is regenerated mechanically by npm run chassis:lock whenever any rostered file changes. It carries no design decision of its own, so amending spec 035 to describe a hash refresh would be an authoring edit with nothing to author. Same waiver as PRs #59, #60, #61 and #62.

title: docs(028,007): the operator manual, and the four things writing it broke
body:
Implements spec 028. Stacked on #61.

`docs/OPERATIONS.md` covers every section of §3.1. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` is restructured by plane with the phase table retired into a build-out history (it had stopped at Phase 6, still named Turso in the thesis, and was missing eight `backend/` directories). `README.md` leads with what this is and how to run it.

§4 item 1's coverage check is `docs/operations-env-coverage.test.ts`: it enumerates `ENRAHITU_*` from source and fails **naming** any variable the table misses, so the table cannot silently rot.

## Writing it broke four things

§1 of the spec predicted a writing exercise. It was not: documenting a claim means executing it.

1. **The image did not build at all.** `scripts/docker-build.sh` assembles a worktree with production `node_modules` only, and `testing/app-harness.ts` imports two devDependency toolchain subpaths that the Encore tsparser walks regardless of `tsconfig` exclude. Pruned. This is the *fourth* instance of one pattern (`frontend/`, `e2e/`, the vitest configs, now `testing/`) and the prune list now says so. It went unnoticed because `image.yml` is cron/dispatch-only, so `main` carries image breakage across green PRs.
2. **The obvious nginx config is wrong for this application.** The OIDC callback sets the access and refresh JWTs as cookies in one response, exceeding nginx's default 4k/8k proxy header buffer. Login completes at the IdP and then dies at the callback with a **502**, while the application log records a successful **302**. The evidence appears only in the proxy's log (`upstream sent too big header`). The nginx example now carries `proxy_buffer_size`; the Ingress example carries the matching annotation because ingress-nginx *is* nginx. Caddy needs nothing, which is the entire difference between those two examples.
3. **The cell must be able to reach its own `ENRAHITU_PUBLIC_URL`.** Server-side OIDC discovery fetches the well-known document from the public origin, so the container hairpins through its own proxy. Where that name does not resolve inside, or its cert is not trusted there, `/api/v1/auth/rauthy/login` returns a bare `500` naming nothing.
4. **A freshly provisioned cell has no control-plane schema**, so its controllers log `no such table: controller_watermark` roughly once a second, forever, until an operator runs `migrate --apply`. Migration being a deploy step is deliberate (spec 027 §3.4); a permanent 1 Hz error loop as the out-of-box state is not. Recorded as a defect for **spec 034** rather than documented away.

## §4 item 2: two of three verified

| Example | Status |
|---|---|
| nginx | **verified** 2026-08-06 |
| Caddy | **verified** 2026-08-06 |
| Kubernetes Ingress | **not verified**: no cluster available |

Verified means: a real password login driven through a real browser engine against the **packaged image** behind that proxy with TLS termination, asserting both token cookies are set and `Secure`, that `/api/v1/auth/me` returns the signed-in operator, and that **no request left the app origin**. The Ingress annotation is derived from the nginx result rather than observed, and both the manual and the spec say so rather than implying a verification that did not happen.

## Also verified here

This branch's image includes #61, so the enc-keys fix got its end-to-end proof in a real container: `secrets.env` carries `ENRAHITU_HIQ_ENC_KEYS`, the exec-ed app process holds it, rauthy's process sees **zero** `ENRAHITU_HIQ_*` variables, and the addon's dev-key warning is gone.

## Sizing

Measured against the packaged arm64 image at N=1, not estimated: 795 MB image, ~210 MiB RSS idle, ~290 MiB after login traffic, ~2 MB volume fresh. Stated floors are 512 MiB and 1 GB. The section says explicitly that it has not been measured under sustained load, and notes that the raft directory grows with *write volume* rather than data size (an idle cell added ~7 MB in an hour).

Full suite: 444 passed, 12 skipped. typecheck, licenses, infra, manifest, chassis, lint all clean.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: chassis.lock is a derived artifact regenerated by `npm run chassis:lock`. It carries no authored intent, and amending spec 035 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration is what .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids. Nothing else is waived: docs/ is spec 028's own territory and takes an authoring amendment there, and scripts/docker-build.sh takes one to spec 007.

title: fix(007,027): the key nothing provisioned, and the secrets that never left the shell
body:
Closes spec 027 §4 item 5, the finding PR #60 recorded rather than fixed.

`docker/first-boot.mjs` generated rauthy's `ENC_KEYS`, both nodes' raft/API secrets, and no encryption key for the app's own hiqlite. The addon fell back to its publicly-known development key, so every cell wrote backup snapshots anyone could decrypt.

## Provisioning the key was half of it

`secrets.env` is *sourced*, and its lines are `NAME='value'` with no `export`. Every name in it was an unexported shell variable. A subshell inherits those, which is why the mistake survives a careful reading: the values are visibly present right up to the last moment. Then `exec` replaces the subshell with the app, and a process environment carries only exported names.

So `ENRAHITU_HIQ_SECRET_RAFT` and `ENRAHITU_HIQ_SECRET_API` had been provisioned on first boot and discarded at `exec` for as long as they have existed: the app's node has been running on the addon's compiled-in defaults for those too. A key added to that file alone would have read as a fix and changed nothing.

## What changed

- **`first-boot.mjs`** generates a key set for the app's node, *separate* from rauthy's. Spec 032's "one key set for both hiqlite instances" is about custody, and custody is unchanged either way: both live in `secrets.env` and spec 027 §3.1 archives the file whole. Sharing the bytes would only mean one compromise decrypts both stores.
- **`entrypoint.sh`** gains `export_hiq_env`, called inside the app's subshell for the reason `export_smtp_env` is called inside rauthy's. Spec 037 §3.1's two-holders rule now covers key material, not just mail credentials.
- **Legacy volumes are named, not migrated.** Provisioning is write-once. Adding a key to an existing volume and activating it would orphan every snapshot already written under the fallback; retaining that fallback so they still decrypt would mean committing a public key to this repo. Neither is worth doing for a volume shape that predates the first release, so the case is reported with its cause and remedy. `export NAME` on an unset name leaves it absent rather than blank, so such a volume still boots.

## What item 5 now means

Item 5's "refuses to start" phrasing is still wrong and is **not** what was fixed: neither store refuses to boot without its keys. What holds now is the substantive half §3.1 builds the single-artifact archive on: the app's snapshots are encrypted under a key unique to that cell, so an app snapshot separated from its `secrets.env` is undecryptable, and the key-binding invariant is true of both stores rather than one. Spec 027 moves to `implementation: complete`.

## Verification

The tests assert *delivery*, not configuration: the environment an `exec`-ed child actually has, plus the negative case that a process which does not export receives none of the material. Both halves were mutation-checked and fail without the fix. Full suite: 440 passed, 12 skipped. typecheck, licenses, infra, manifest, chassis, lint all clean.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: chassis.lock is a derived artifact regenerated by `npm run chassis:lock`. It carries no authored intent, and amending spec 035 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration is what .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids. Nothing else is waived: docker/first-boot.mjs, docker/entrypoint.sh and both test files are spec 007's own territory and take an authoring amendment there, and spec 027 takes one for the finding it recorded.

title: feat(027,009): the three verbs, and the key nothing provisions
body:
Spec 027's remaining verbs land under `scripts/ops/`, and `template.toml` carries all four at contract **v0.8.0**. One bump rather than four: they are one vocabulary, and a factory adopting them one at a time would pass through three versions in which it could operate a stamped app halfway, with a `backup` and no `restore` being the version that matters.

## The verbs

**`migrate` owns no migration logic.** The runner and both drivers are TS whose value imports the bundler resolves and plain node does not, and the verbs run in the packaged image with no transpiler, so a script-shaped half would be a second runner for a property whose entire value is that there is one. The verb is the transport over both stores' admin pairs.

**`backup`** is cold by default and hot with `--online`. The hot path captures the resource store first and the chain last, which is the whole of §3.2's consistency answer: three processes with three write paths cannot be made one instant, and the skew is asymmetric. A chain holding a Decision for a row the resource member lacks is visible; a row whose admitting Decision is absent is not. The manifest records a captured-at per member so the ordering is auditable rather than promised.

The archive is organised by §3.1's four state classes, which `/data` is not: `/data/rauthy` holds two of them. Key material is gathered from both directories into one member and placed back into both. A directory copy would have restored rauthy's encryption keys *with* rauthy's store, and the binding argument that makes this one artifact would have held by accident.

**`restore`** verifies every checksum before touching the volume, and forks on the member's shape. A hot archive's hiqlite members are snapshot files, staged and armed through the two scoped variables; a cold archive's are the raft directories themselves, placed as they are, because a stopped node's directory IS the state it recovers from and manufacturing a backup file from it would discard exactly that. §3.3 has one name for both shapes because it was written when the app's hiqlite was to be recreated empty.

The lock and owner record are stripped on the way in: a restored volume has no previous owner. That is also why liveness is asked of the app's listening port rather than of the volume. The addon never releases `state_machine/lock`, so it is present on every *stopped* cell, and a verb reading it as a liveness signal would refuse every cold backup it was asked for.

## Run against the real topology

Items 2, 3, 9 and 10 are no longer deferred. A populated cell (four members, four tiers, 59 chained Decisions) was backed up **cold with the container stopped** and **hot while it served**; each archive was restored into a fresh volume and a cell booted on it. Both came up, verified the chain to the same head (`decision-000059`), and served the same members and tiers, including a tier created minutes before the backup. rauthy came up on the restored store and served OIDC discovery through the app's own origin. The hot restore was applied through the two scoped variables, with the entrypoint log showing each node offered exactly its own file: item 9 against a running container rather than a harness.

It found three things no unit test could:

1. **A session is not enough for an unsafe method.** The admin plane double-submits CSRF, and signing in does not issue the csrf cookie: `GET /api/v1/auth/csrf-token` does. A verb presenting only a session is refused on every POST. The verbs now perform the same two-step the SPA performs.
2. **The model's identity is its canonical `integrity.hash`, not a digest of `app-model.json`'s bytes.** Hashing the file produced a different number of the same shape, so §3.3's upgrade warning fired on every restore, including one into the identical image.
3. The third is not a defect in these verbs.

## §4 item 5 is disproven, not merely unmet

§3.1 says the app's hiqlite encrypts its snapshots with `ENRAHITU_HIQ_ENC_KEYS` "from the same file" and concludes the key binding "is now true twice over". **Nothing provisions that variable.** `docker/first-boot.mjs` writes rauthy's encryption keys and both nodes' raft secrets, and no encryption key for the app's node, so the addon falls back to its publicly-known development key and warns on every boot.

Demonstrated: a cold archive restored into a fresh volume with **all key material deleted** served every member. The resource store opened without the keys the archive carried, because the key that would have stopped it is not one this substrate ever generates. Item 5's first half did not hold as stated either: rauthy starts cleanly against a store encrypted under a key it no longer has, because its at-rest encryption covers particular columns and surfaces at first decrypt rather than at boot.

The larger consequence is not a backup defect: **every cell stores the association's data, and writes its snapshots, under a key that is public.** The verbs only made it visible, which is what §3.8 says a spec ahead of its code is for.

**Left for a decision rather than fixed here.** Provisioning the key is one line in a file spec 007 owns, but doing it to a volume that already holds data written under the development key is a key-rotation question with a data-loss edge, and `secrets.env` is written once and never rewritten. `implementation` stays `in-progress` on item 5 alone; every other acceptance item now holds.

## Verification

`npm run typecheck` and `npm test` green (431 passed, 34 files), including 25 new tests across the archive round trip (cold and hot, the tamper refusal with the volume untouched, both liveness refusals, the 0600 archive, the world-readable destination, remote-ledger detection, capture order, both degraded credentials reporting the age of what they ship) and the migrate transport (both stores, the CSRF acquisition, the three admin-plane refusals told apart). `check:manifest`, `check:model`, `check:chassis`, `check:infra` and `check:licenses` clean; `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: chassis.lock is a derived artifact regenerated by `npm run chassis:lock`. It carries no authored intent, and amending spec 035 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration is what .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids. Nothing else is waived: scripts/ops/ is spec 027's own territory, and template.toml takes an authoring amendment to spec 009 alongside 027's.

title: feat(027,007,023,021,025): the backup plane, and one variable two nodes both read
body:
Spec 027 §3.2 and §3.3, ahead of the scripts. Both are reaches past the volume into a running process, which no script can supply itself, so a verb written before them would be a verb written against a guess.

## The admin plane's backup pair

`POST /api/admin/state/backups` creates and names; `GET` lists. Gated through `requireOperator()` like the two schema pairs beside them, and there for the reason the schema verb is there, generalized by §3.4's 2026-08-04 settlement: at N=1 the app's embedded hiqlite node holds the volume open, so an operation on that store is performed BY the running app under an authenticated operator, or it is not performed at all. A cold backup needs neither endpoint, because a stopped node's directory is already the state it would recover from.

The `admin` service's ceiling grows by `cap.backup.state.write` and `cap.backup.state.list`, which spec 032 declared and no service held.

**One thing the build had to add that the spec did not ask for.** `backup()` returns void, so the file name is read back from the listing, and the listing is read **before as well as after**. The addon's sixty-second duplicate-request guard is silent: a second request inside the window returns the first snapshot with nothing to say so. Without the before-reading the endpoint cannot tell a fresh snapshot from a suppressed one, and §3.6's promise to report the age of what the verb ships is unanswerable at exactly the moment it matters. The response carries `fresh` for that.

## One variable, two nodes, and the addon confirms it

§3.3 called this live in the tree rather than hypothetical, and the addon's own binary settles it: the app's hiqlite reads `HQL_BACKUP_RESTORE`, an unprefixed name, while every other setting it takes is `ENRAHITU_HIQ_*`. rauthy's embedded node reads the same name. One ambient value naming one file was read by two independent state machines, and whichever node it was not meant for either refuses the file or, worse, accepts it.

Each store now gets its own variable: `ENRAHITU_RESTORE_RAUTHY` and `ENRAHITU_RESTORE_APP`. `first-boot.mjs` records a decision per store and writes two scoped lines into `restore.env`; the entrypoint maps exactly one onto `HQL_BACKUP_RESTORE` inside the owning process's subshell and drops both prefixed names there. **The app moved into a subshell of its own** to receive one, which it never needed before: it started at top level, where an export is visible to everything started after it. `exec` keeps `$APP_PID` the process the traps signal, so die-together is unchanged.

Two decisions the design left open, settled by building it:

- **An ambient `HQL_BACKUP_RESTORE` is named and ignored, not honoured and not fatal.** Honouring it means choosing a store, and choosing wrong offers rauthy's snapshot to the app's node. Refusing to boot over it is worse than it sounds: the name is hiqlite's own, so an orchestrator exporting it for an unrelated workload would take this container down. first-boot names it in the log, the entrypoint scrubs it, which is the shape spec 026 §3.1 already used for an inherited `SMTP_*`.
- **A pre-split marker is carried forward under `legacy`, not interpreted.** It recorded one decision for one ambient variable and cannot say which store it meant.

## An ownership move, not a waiver

`docker/first-boot.test.ts` moves from spec 025's `establishes` to spec 007's. Spec 025 established it for §3.4's `/metrics` token assertions; it has since become the test file for everything `first-boot.mjs` does, so ownership followed the first spec to need a test file rather than the script under test. Every later change to a spec-007 script therefore arrived as drift against a spec-025 path, asking a network-hardening spec to authorize restore semantics it has no view on. Spec 025's assertions are unchanged and remain its acceptance; only authority over the path moved. Both specs record the transfer and the reason.

Spec 027's `## 4. Acceptance` heading is also restored: it was lost in an earlier amendment, leaving the eleven items inside §3.8.

## Verification

`npm run typecheck` and `npm test` green (406 passed, 32 files), including 13 new tests: three on the backup surface against a booted node (a real snapshot on the volume, the guard window returning the same file, and the denial for a service the manifest does not grant it to), six on per-store first-boot bookkeeping, and four asserting the entrypoint's **actual environment** in two subshells, because the failure §3.3 guards is inheritance rather than logic. `check:manifest`, `check:model`, `check:chassis`, `check:infra` and `check:licenses` clean; `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0.

What remains of 027: `backup`, `restore` and `migrate` as scripts under `scripts/ops/`, and the four `[verbs]` entries with the contract bump to 0.8.0.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: chassis.lock is a derived artifact regenerated by `npm run chassis:lock`. It carries no authored intent, and amending spec 035 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration is what .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids. Nothing else is waived: the first-boot test file's drift was resolved by moving its ownership to the spec that owns the script it tests, and every other path takes an authoring amendment to specs 027, 007, 023, 021 or 025.

title: feat(027,021,023,004): CoreLedger's half of migrate, and the loser that never said so
body:
Stacked on #57 (base is `feat/027-preflight`; it retargets to main when #57 merges). Spec 027 §3.4's CoreLedger half, which §3.7 named as the next step.

## Where it lands, and why not in a script

The volume argument that put the state layer's half on the operator plane does not carry here: a libSQL file admits other processes and a Postgres ledger is remote by definition, which is why §3.4 kept this half script-shaped. Two other reasons put it there anyway.

1. **A script-shaped half would have to be a second runner.** `migrate()` and both drivers are TS whose value imports the bundler resolves and plain node does not, and the verbs run in the packaged image with production dependencies and no transpiler. A second copy of a runner whose entire value is "exactly once" is the duplication #57 had just removed from the entrypoint.
2. **A migration is an act, and an act has an actor.** Through this plane it is authenticated, role-gated and adjudicated, so it lands on the Decision chain naming a principal rather than happening anonymously on somebody's shell.

`GET /api/admin/ledger/schema` and `POST /api/admin/ledger/schema/apply` mirror the state pair exactly.

## Two grants, not four

The admin service gains `cap.db.app.migrate` and `cap.db.app.read`, mirroring what it already holds for the state layer.

The runner reaches the driver's `query`, `execute` and `transaction`, which the seam adjudicates as `db.read`, `db.write` and `db.txn`. Running it through the governed driver would therefore have meant granting the admin service write and transaction access over the whole application ledger in order to migrate it, which is write access with a migration-shaped name. So `Ledger.migrate()` demands `db.migrate` on `app` once and drives the runner against the driver from before the wrap: the same shape and the same argument spec 032 §3.6 already used for the state layer. `Ledger.fromEnv()` keeps the raw reference it already constructed, so this is one more use inside the file that always had one, not a new site.

## Two premises the build falsified

**The concurrent loser does not report a constraint violation.** §3.4 said it does, on the migrations table's primary key. It fails earlier, inside its own `up()`, because the winner already created the table the migration creates, and SQLite says "table already exists". A seam recognising the loser by matching constraint text would have handled the case the spec imagined and missed the case that happens. So the seam asks a fact instead: on any failure it re-reads the applied set, and if every declared version is recorded, the failure was caused by work another runner had already done and nothing is half-applied. If any version is still missing, the original error is rethrown untouched.

The test is a real race, not a simulated one: the loser is held at the exact window between its read of applied versions and its first transaction, and released once the winner has committed. It found the above on its first run.

**`ENRAHITU_MIGRATE_ON_BOOT` did not "remain" available.** §3.4's wording read as a description of something built; nothing implemented it. It exists now, default false, on `backend/auth/store.ts`, which is the only place anything opens the ledger at boot and therefore the only boot seam CoreLedger has.

## Verification

`npm run typecheck` and `npm test` green (393 passed, 31 files), including six new tests on the seam: the version report that does not create the table it reports on, apply-once, apply-nothing-twice, the held-open race, and the denial for a service the manifest does not grant it to. `check:manifest`, `check:model`, `check:chassis`, `check:infra` and `check:licenses` clean; `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0.

It carries no authored intent, and amending spec 035 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration is what .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids. title: feat(027,007): the pre-flight verb, and the port that was never 8080
body:
Spec 027 §3.5's first verb, plus the declared migration home §3.4 asks for. `scripts/ops/` was an established path with nothing in it; it now holds `preflight.mjs`.

## What it checks

Six conditions, before anything starts, with the entrypoint calling it under `set -e`:

| condition | verdict |
|---|---|
| every name in `ENRAHITU_REQUIRED_ENV` is set and non-empty | judged |
| `ENRAHITU_PUBLIC_URL` parses, and its scheme is one the entrypoint's cookie-mode branch understands | judged |
| the data directory is writable by the runtime user | judged |
| the ledger URL's scheme maps to a driver | judged |
| every port the entrypoint will bind is free | judged |
| plain http on a non-loopback host | reported |
| pending migrations exist or do not | reported |

The judged/reported split is §3.5's own. Plain http off loopback is a real deployment behind someone else's TLS terminator, and the pending-migration count is what a deploy step acts on rather than a precondition of booting. Neither blocks a boot; both are said out loud.

Spec 007's `ENRAHITU_REQUIRED_ENV` loop moves INTO the verb rather than sitting beside it. The fleet-facing contract is unchanged in every respect a fleet can see; what changed is that it has one implementation instead of two, and the copy in bash was the one nothing could test.

## What building it corrected

§3.5 said the ports to check are "8080, 8081, and the hiqlite pairs". The app's listener is not a constant: the Encore runtime takes `ENCORE_LISTEN_ADDR`, then `PORT`, then 8080, so the packaged image binds 8080 and the dev topology (spec 033) binds 4000. A verb checking the constant would have passed over the port the dev container was about to take and reported on one nothing wanted, which is a pre-flight that reads green for the wrong reason. The verb derives the app's address from the environment; rauthy's three stay constants because they are constants.

## What it settled for the next step

`backend/core/ledger/migration-list.ts` is the home `migrate()` has lacked since spec 011 landed a runner with no list. Its module-level imports must stay type-only, because the pre-flight reads the declared versions before the app is a process and loads the file under Node's own type stripping.

That constraint also bounds what step 2 can do: applying a migration reaches `migrate()` and both drivers, whose value imports the bundler resolves and plain node does not. So CoreLedger's half of the `migrate` verb lands on the admin plane, as the state layer's half already did, or as a second runner in JS. §3.7 records it as a fork with its constraint known rather than an assumption.

The four `[verbs]` entries and the contract bump to 0.8.0 land once all four verbs exist, rather than four times.

## Verification

`npm run typecheck` and `npm test` green (387 passed, 30 files). Item 8's conditions are verified one at a time in `scripts/ops/preflight.test.ts`; its second half ("the entrypoint refuses to continue") runs the real prologue against a stub `node` in `docker/entrypoint.test.ts`, so fail-closed is executed rather than described. `check:infra`, `check:manifest`, `check:chassis`, `check:licenses` and the model gate all clean; `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0.

title: spec(027): the state layer is not derived, and the archive has a third member
body:
## Summary

027 was written on 2026-07-25 and picked up on 2026-08-04, and the thing it was
written about changed underneath it. This amends it before anything is built,
because two of its load-bearing claims are now false and one of them is
destructive.

**§3.1 said the app's hiqlite "is deliberately not backed up: its entire contents
are the cache with TTLs and rate-limit counters, both derived and both correct to
lose". §3.3 said restore "recreates this directory empty".** Both were true when
written: spec 002's hiqlite was a cache, and the addon's whole surface was nine
functions with no snapshot primitive, which the spec enumerated to show the
exclusion was forced rather than chosen.

Then phase 2 took the addon to twenty-one functions and added `backup()`, phase 3
put the control plane's `resource` table behind it, and phase 5 filled that table
with the association. The sentence did not change and its meaning inverted:
*deliberately not backed up* went from describing a cache to describing the
primary store. Built as written, `backup` would have produced an archive with no
members, tiers, memberships or dues in it, and `restore` would have deleted them.
Both would have passed their own acceptance tests, because those tests were
written from the same sentence.

**The second defect is live in the tree rather than hypothetical.**
`HQL_BACKUP_RESTORE` is hiqlite's variable, not rauthy's, and the app runs an
embedded hiqlite too. `restore.env` is sourced before either supervised process
starts and its own comment states the reason: *"both hiqlite instances would
otherwise inherit it."* One value naming one file is read by two independent
nodes with two unrelated state machines. It is latent only because the app's
store has held nothing worth restoring, which is the same premise defect wearing
a different hat. The fix is spec 037 §3.1's scoping pattern applied to the same
file: the entrypoint scopes each restore variable into exactly the subshell that
should act on it.

**The hot path has no cross-store consistency point, so the ordering is the
answer.** Three stores, three processes, no shared transaction. The skew is
asymmetric because the Decision chain lives in CoreLedger and the resources those
Decisions admit live in hiqlite: a Decision naming an absent resource still
verifies and is visible, while a resource with no Decision is an unaudited row,
which is the one thing the kernel plane exists to prevent and is invisible. So
the resource store is snapshotted first and the chain last, putting the skew
permanently in the detectable direction. The manifest gains a per-member
captured-at instant so this is auditable after the fact rather than promised.

Also settled: the admin plane becomes the transport for the hot backup, because
*"at N=1 the app holds the volume open, so the operation must be performed by the
running app under an authenticated operator"* is a property of the volume, not of
migration, so the 2026-07-30 amendment's reasoning governs backup identically
rather than being re-derived.

`implementation` stays **pending**. No verb is built and `scripts/ops/` is still
an established path with nothing in it. §3.7 records exactly what remains and
flags that acceptance items 2, 3 and 5 need a compose-level fixture rather than
the app harness, because a cold backup is defined by the container being stopped.

§3.8 is the part worth reading if you read one section: a spec ahead of its code
decays in a way a spec behind it does not. Spec 001 §5.2's disposition table
catches the lagging case and has no column for the leading one, and 027 led by
nine days across three phases. The cheap guard is to re-read a pending spec's
**premises**, not just its design, at the moment somebody picks it up. The design
was fine; the facts under it were not, and no gate can see that.

Contract bump target corrected to 0.8.0 (0.7.0 was spent by spec 015).

## Testing

Specs only, no code. compile 39 specs 0 warnings, `lint --fail-on-warn` clean,
index fresh, `check:chassis` fresh.

title: fix(033): the harness waits for readiness, not for a listener
body:
## Summary

`startApp` polled `/healthz` to decide the app was up, and spec 025's probe
separation is exactly why that was the wrong question. Liveness touches no
dependency **by design**, so `/healthz` answers 200 the moment the listener
opens, while the hiqlite raft election that spec 033 §3.1 already calls the
dominant cost of boot is still running. The harness handed back an instance that
was serving and not ready, and the remainder of the boot was paid by whichever
request came first, inside whatever test happened to make it, against vitest's
five-second default rather than the ninety-second budget `beforeAll` was given.

It passed for six weeks because the gap was under five seconds. The gap is not a
constant: it grows with every domain that registers kinds and starts controllers
at boot, and specs 036, 037 and 004 each widened it. It crossed on #54, a branch
that touches no code at all, and surfaced as a timeout on an unrelated assertion
about the mock auth driver being absent in production.

The shape worth recording, and why the amendment is prose rather than a one-line
diff note: **a readiness check that is merely usually fast is a deadline nobody
declared.** It fails first in CI, on whichever test is unlucky, naming something
that has nothing to do with it. The failing assertion was about auth drivers; the
defect was in the boot gate.

`/readyz` checks the ledger and hiqlite, so `startApp` now returns when the app
can serve rather than when it can listen, and the wait sits inside the boot
budget where it was always supposed to be.

Spec 033 §3.1 carries the dated amendment.

## Testing

The assertion that was timing out at 5003ms in CI now runs in **4ms**:

```
✓ production mode disables the mock driver > does not advertise the mock driver 4ms
✓ production mode disables the mock driver > refuses the mock login route 2ms
```

Full suite locally: 29 files, 346 passed, 12 skipped. typecheck clean. compile 38
specs 0 warnings, `lint --fail-on-warn` clean, index fresh, `check:chassis` fresh.

Merge this before #54, which is red only on this defect.

title: spec(038): board governance, and the roll that has to stop moving
body:
Spec 036 shipped one domain completely on the bet that the remaining domains are
the same shape and the shape is what has to be right. A bet stated in the spec
that makes it is not evidence, so this is the second domain, and its first job is
to be ordinary: five kinds (`officer`, `meeting`, `motion`, `ballot`, `minutes`),
one two-loop controller on `ctl:governance`, a `governance` service holding the
same six grants `members` holds, and no new machinery in `backend/control/`. It
is a spec ahead of its code, like 026, 030 and 037 were, because three of its
decisions change what gets built and are cheaper to argue now.

## Summary

**A meeting freezes its roll and its rule at the call.** Memberships lapse on a
calendar (036 §3.7) and bylaws get amended, so an electorate evaluated when it is
needed is different on the day of the meeting than on the day it was called, and
different again on the day somebody reads the minute. A quorum recomputed at the
tally therefore produces a minute that says a motion carried and a recomputation
two years later that says the meeting was inquorate, and nothing flags the
disagreement, because both computations are correct about their own moment. That
is what a record date is for in every association's bylaws and it is what it is
here. The roll rides in `spec` rather than `status`, because putting it in
`status` would create the one field in the corpus that must never be recomputed,
sitting in the column every reconciler is written to recompute. That in turn
forces the call to be a transition rather than an edit (`draft` then `called`),
which is what an association does anyway.

**A ballot is named `<motion>-<member>`.** One vote per member is structural
rather than checked, because the second cast is the same resource as the first.
This is 036's `invoiceNameFor` in a second domain, and its recurrence is the
point: twice now a domain's correctness has come from choosing a name instead of
writing a guard. A voter may recast while the poll is open, and what the chain
preserves is stated narrowly enough that nobody over-trusts it later:
`contextHash` is a hash, so the ledger proves that a ballot changed and by whom,
and does not preserve what it said before.

**Eligibility is refused at the endpoint and decided again at the tally.** Not
036 §3.3's reasoning, which is worth recording because reusing it is the obvious
move: the roll is frozen here, so an admission-time check would actually hold.
The real reason is that `admit` takes an actor string and not a session, so "is
this caller on the roll" is a question only the edge can ask, and the tally is
the only backstop for every ballot that did not arrive through it.

This is also the spec that spends what 034 §3.7 has been carrying for two specs
without a consumer. Casting a ballot is the first member-plane write in the
substrate, so an ordinary member's subject appears as a Decision actor for the
first time, which is what makes the chain a voting record rather than an
operations log. §3.11 is then honest about the half it does not cover: the
endpoint refusals are application logic and not a ceiling, since `db.txn` on
`state` is every kind in one table, so the record cannot be quietly changed but
it can be changed. That is worth more than an immutability claim this substrate
cannot make, and it gives spec 020 §3.4's per-kind grant extension the stated
consumer that 034 §3.3 and 036 §5 both carried without one.

Bounded deliberately, with the boundaries argued rather than deferred: elections
are out (generalizing the ballot from a question to a choice among candidates
brings ranked voting, ties, runoffs and per-seat counting, a domain's worth of
second-order questions); quorum is over ballots cast rather than attendance, and
§3.2 says so plainly instead of implying otherwise; abstentions count toward
quorum and not toward the threshold, with the worked example showing the same
ballots carrying one way and failing the other; and a motion's only
machine-readable effect is minutes approval, because the moment a motion can
change one piece of state the next request is a motion that can change any piece.

It amends two specs, declared in §2 and not yet made: spec 036 §3.1, where the
`tenant` kind gains the association's bylaws constants, and spec 037, which gains
one chassis template. 036 §5 is corrected here to name 038 as the owner of board
governance and to record that the shape held.

## Testing

warnings; index fresh; `check:chassis` fresh; typecheck clean. No code changes:
`implementation: pending`.

title: feat(004,036,001): the session adapter, and the clock that had to be rauthy's
body:
Spec 001 §5.3's thin adapter. rauthy owns authentication **and** principal identity; this service keeps the same-origin httpOnly cookie shell, the CSRF double-submit and rate limiting, and gives up everything else.

## The defect this fixes, which nothing could see from outside

The session's subject was a locally minted `UserAccount` id. rauthy's own `sub` was filed away as `ssoProviderId` and never reached the token.

So the principal binding spec 001 §5.3 describes, and which spec 036 §3.8 uses to answer *"which member record is yours"*, **could never match**. That branch was dead code, and every member-plane lookup fell through to matching on an email address that nothing had verified: no `email_verified` was carried, and `preferred_username` (a display handle several providers let the user choose) stood in for a missing address. The safety argument for that fallback was written in a comment and implemented nowhere.

Now the subject is the IdP's `sub`, `email_verified` is threaded and required by the fallback, and `preferred_username` links nothing.

## The clock

rauthy stamps every refresh token with

    nbf = issued + access_token_lifetime - 60      # token_set.rs

so it cannot be used until sixty seconds before its access token expires. The app minted a fixed 15-minute token against rauthy's default 30, so **every renewal would have arrived before `nbf`, been refused with `Token is not valid yet`, and logged every user out at fifteen minutes, permanently, in production only.**

The app now mints its access token with the lifetime rauthy reports in `expires_in`. Following the authority's clock is the same decision as following its `sub`: if rauthy owns the session, it owns when the session ends.

This was found end-to-end and could not have been found any other way. Every unit test passed throughout, before and after.

## What retired

`UserAccount` and `RefreshToken`, with `user-model.ts` and `refresh-token-model.ts`. Each was a second opinion about a question the IdP already answers, and the refresh table meant an administrator revoking a user at rauthy left them logged in here.

The tables are **deliberately not dropped**: they are the only record of who logged in before the cutover. `AuditLog` survives, and its records now name the same person by two identifiers either side of the cutover, which spec 004 §3.6 records rather than leaves to be discovered. Every session in flight is invalidated once.

## The e2e was broken on main

Since 2026-07-29, when spec 015's React convergence moved the driver list from `/` to `/login`. `e2e.yml` is nightly and dispatch-only, so the PR gate never saw it: a check that does not gate a merge will eventually be red without anybody knowing. Fixed here, routed through the landing page, and extended to cover renewal by decoding the renewed token and asserting `exp - iat` equals the IdP's lifetime.

The dev client's `access_token_lifetime` drops 1800 → 60 so that window opens immediately; at 1800 renewal could only have been exercised after idling 29 minutes, which is why it was never exercised at all.

## Verification

346 unit tests, typecheck, compile, index, lint green. The browser-real login e2e passes: login, `/me`, **renewal**, CSRF logout, RP-initiated logout, 401 afterwards, all on one origin.

Neither carries authored intent, and amending spec 035 or spec 006 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration is what .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids. Nothing else is waived: backend/auth/, backend/lib/, backend/members/, docker/rauthy/, e2e/ and frontend/ all take authoring amendments to specs 004, 036, 001, 005, 015 and 017.

title: feat(037,036,020,021): application mail, and the kind the consumer could not invent
body:
Spec 036 shipped a renewal controller that knows a member owes money on a date and had no way to tell them. This is the channel, plus the scheduling half that decides when it speaks.

## A notice is a resource, not a function call

Sending is not idempotent and everything else here is, so delivery is reconciliation over a `mailNotice` and idempotence comes from the same place it comes from everywhere else: **the name**. `dues-reminder-<invoice>` raised a hundred times is one notice, so a controller that crashes mid-pass and re-reconciles from a reset watermark sends nothing twice. Nothing awaits a relay inside a request.

Retry is a status rather than a queue. After six attempts a notice is `failed` and **stays readable** at `GET /api/notices`, because a notice that gave up silently is worse than one that was never raised: the treasurer believes the member was told. Retrying by hand is deliberately not offered, since a re-send button is a button that mails somebody their third copy.

A second loop drives retry for the same reason spec 036 needs a calendar sweep: a deferred retry is not a write, so the change feed can never deliver "this notice's backoff has elapsed".

## The kind the consumer could not invent

Spec 037 was written as though `smtp.egress` were a string this repo could choose. **It is not**, and finding that out is the most useful thing in this change. It took three layers: the `capKind` enum in `contracts/` (here), the toolchain's extractor (unchanged), and the kernel's kind table compiled into the `kernel-native` binary, which refuses to boot a model declaring a kind it cannot classify.

That refusal is spec 021's ceiling working as designed: a new effect family cannot be introduced by the consumer at all. It took an upstream change and a published release (statecrafting#17, `kernel-native` 0.2.0, tag v0.9.0).

The tempting shortcut was to route mail through `http.egress` and move on. That buys a green build by describing an SMTP socket as an HTTP request in the audit record, which is worse than having no capability: **an ungoverned channel is visible, a mislabelled one is not.**

## What the extractor caught

`backend/members/` importing the mail barrel failed model verification:

    service 'members' uses http.egress (via backend/mail/transport.ts) beyond its declared ceiling

The barrel re-exported the transport, so the domain inherited its egress ceiling. The fix is `backend/mail/notice.ts`, holding `raiseNotice` and reaching nothing but the store. The fix NOT taken was granting `members` the capability, which would have turned the build green in one line and made the whole design ornamental: a domain that can reach the transport can send inside a request. A comment in the barrel was actively denying a coupling the import graph had; that boundary is now checked on every build.

## Two mail surfaces, and two holders

`ENRAHITU_MAIL_*` is the application's and `ENRAHITU_SMTP_*` stays rauthy's. Reusing the latter would have required un-scoping it from the rauthy subshell, dismantling the invariant spec 026 exists to establish, silently.

Prefixing alone does not achieve that, because a subshell inherits the whole environment. The entrypoint now drops each surface at the point the other process no longer needs it, and the order is the guarantee.

## The rest

- Templates: chassis defaults, `app/mail/templates/` overrides, silently and by design. That is the **opposite** of the manifest overlay's rule, and the asymmetry is the point: a template carries no privilege. The cost is stated in `app/mail/README.md` at the moment somebody makes the trade.
- One source renders text and HTML. A missing parameter is refused rather than mailed as a literal `{{amount}}`.
- `none` is the default and not a testing convenience: notices are raised and held, so turning mail on later delivers the backlog.
- A minimal SMTP client rather than a mailer dependency. It refuses a relay with no STARTTLS unless told the network is private, and it dot-stuffs, which is the bug that truncates a message at any body line consisting of a single dot.

## Spec 036's half

§3.10 decides **when**, which 037 left to the domain: one reminder on the branch that raises the invoice, one receipt on the branch that renews the term, both named for the invoice. The pure rule returns an intent; the controller resolves the recipient. A notice that cannot be raised is logged and does not fail the reconcile.

## Verification

344 tests green, typecheck, model, manifest, infra, licenses, compile, index and lint clean.

Verified end to end in the dev topology against Mailpit: an expired membership raised its invoice and a reminder arrived from the configured sender with both parts rendered; two further sweeps delivered nothing; a backdated payment extended the term to 2027-01-01 and produced exactly one receipt.

Two things stated rather than implied: the socket ban is asserted as an in-repo test rather than in the toolchain's extraction ban-list, so it protects this repo and not a stamped app (§3.7 records the follow-up); and a tier carries no currency, so a notice reads "dues of 45.00" with no symbol (spec 036 §5).

Nothing else is waived: backend/mail/, backend/members/, backend/kernel/egress.ts, backend/lib/, contracts/, docker/entrypoint.sh and docker/compose.yml all take authoring amendments to specs 037, 036, 021, 020, 004, 007 and 033.

title: spec(036): the loop nothing writes, and the row that could stop it
body:
Spec 036 was marked `implementation: complete` while staying silent on several behaviors the code depends on, and while describing one it does not implement. This makes it describe what is actually built, and fixes the one defect that writing it down turned up.

## What the spec did not say

- **The calendar sweep.** A change feed cannot observe the passage of time: a membership whose term expires tomorrow is not written tomorrow, so a purely change-driven controller would lapse nobody until somebody happened to edit their row. The second loop, its hourly interval, and the shared lease key that keeps the two from superseding each other were all undocumented.
- **Three branches of the renewal rule**: a lifetime tier carrying `endsOn`, a billed tier missing it, and a voided invoice.
- **That terms are UTC-anchored calendar days** rather than instants, and that advancing a period clamps to month end, so a monthly term dated the 31st does not skip February and drift a month a year.
- **Which startup failures are fatal.** Only a tenant mismatch exits the process; everything else leaves the application serving with the domain answering 503, because a subsystem's failure may not remove the instruments used to diagnose it. Also that the association record is create-if-absent, so a restart cannot reset an operator's chosen display name back to the slug.
- `/api/org`, the tier and member deletes, and the void endpoint.

## What it said that was not true

The member plane resolves a member by `sub` and then falls back to the session's email. The spec described `sub` alone, which made acceptance item 9 read as a stronger guarantee than the code provides.

Section 3.8 now states the actual rule and names the weakness in it: nothing checks `email_verified`, and the SSO profile substitutes `preferred_username` when the email claim is absent, which is not an email and is not verified under any provider. Against rauthy this is latent rather than live, since rauthy proves control of the address before a session exists at all, but it rests on a property of the IdP's configuration rather than on anything this code enforces. Closing it belongs to spec 004's rewrite, where the session's claims are minted and where enrollment can write `sub` at first login.

## The defect

`sweepOnce` had no per-membership error isolation. The enumeration is ordered, so one unreconcilable row aborted the whole pass and every membership after it silently went unbilled, every hour, with dues that simply never appear as the only symptom. It now logs the row and continues, which is safe precisely because the sweep keeps no watermark and re-lists from the top next pass.

## Tests

The sweep and the boot path had no coverage at all. Both have it now, including the property that a row which cannot reconcile does not stop the memberships that sort after it.

title: fix(002): ownership stops being keyed on the hostname
body:
PR #46's lock recovery had a hole big enough to reproduce the outage it was
written to prevent, and it was found the way the original was: by using the
container for a session and then looking. `/readyz` had been answering **500 for
seven hours** with `/healthz` green, and the membership surface 503 for exactly
as long.

```
hiq: state-machine lock left in place  reason=foreign-host  ownerHost=2763aec70bc1
thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked: Lock file already exists: /data/hiqlite/state_machine/lock
members: runtime did not start; the membership surface will answer 503
```

**In docker the hostname IS the container id.** `up --build`, a `restart`, an
image change and a rescheduled pod all produce a new one, so the previous
owner's record looked like it came from another machine. The `foreign-host`
branch did what it was told, kept the lock, and hiqlite panicked. Every container
recreate was unrecoverable without a human deleting a file inside the container,
which is the original defect verbatim.

## The hostname was answering two questions badly

| question | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| Is this my data directory? | hostname | `node`, the node's **configured** identity |
| Can I interpret that pid? | hostname | `ns`, the pid namespace |
| Is that pid the same process? | not asked | `start`, from `/proc/<pid>/stat` |

`node` comes from configuration and deliberately **not** from the volume: an
identity minted into the data directory is read by whoever opens it and therefore
matches by construction, which is a check with no content. Configured
(`ENRAHITU_HIQ_NODE_ID`, 1 at N=1, the ordinal at N=3, spec 030's
`HQL_NODE_ID_FROM=k8s` when it lands), it catches something nothing caught
before: **node 2 booting against node 1's PVC**, which at N=3 is catastrophic and
used to look like a normal start.

## Two findings from verifying it

Both changed the design rather than decorating it.

1. **The namespace inode is not a reliable discriminator.** Linux reuses
   namespace inode numbers, and a forced recreate was observed reporting the
   identical `pid:[4026533958]` as the container it replaced. A design resting on
   the namespace alone would have been correct in the test and wrong in the
   field.
2. **A recreated container reuses low pids immediately.** The replacement came up
   as **pid 94**. A stale record naming a low pid would find it alive and keep
   the lock on a coincidence.

So the record also carries `start`, the owner's process start time. A pid whose
start time changed is a different process wearing a reused number. That is what
makes recovery reliable rather than lucky.

## Fallbacks stay safe in the direction that preserves the guard

- No procfs, or a record predating the field: the pid alone decides, as before.
- A legacy record is read **on its old terms**, comparing hostnames, so the
  single boot after an upgrade still refuses to clear a lock a live process on
  this machine holds, while a legacy record from a recreated container recovers
  instead of stranding. Both directions are asserted.

Not protected, and stated rather than pretended: two live containers mounting one
data directory. The previous version did not protect it either, it merely
declined to decide, and spec 030 §3.4 forbids the topology outright (per-pod PVC,
never shared).

## Verified against the running container

A forced recreate changed the container id `6a38b899aa0a` → `25fa7fb4412b`, and
the successor cleared the lock on its own:

```
hiq: cleared a stale state-machine lock  reason=owner-gone  previousPid=612
members: runtime started
readyz HTTP 200
```

The suite was also run **inside the linux container**, which is where the
pid-reuse branch is reachable at all. That caught two things macOS hides: a test
helper silently dropping the very field under test (so the case would have passed
vacuously here and failed on CI), and this suite reading
`ENRAHITU_HIQ_DATA_DIR` from the ambient environment, which pointed the
no-data-directory case at a **real volume** and could have deleted a live node's
lock. The env is now cleared for the duration.

title: spec(037): application mail, and the transport the kernel could not see
body:
Spec 026 gave the IdP a mail path and named exactly what application mail would
need: "an outbox and a sender identity." Spec 036 then shipped a renewal
controller that knows a member owes money on a date and has no way to tell them.
This supplies both.

**A spec ahead of its code**, like 026 and 030 were, because three of its
decisions change what gets built and are much cheaper to argue now than after.

## The kernel gains a second transport

`backend/kernel/egress.ts` is the only module in `backend/` permitted a bare
`fetch`, and it adjudicates `http.egress` on every call. That model is
HTTP-shaped. An SMTP transport opens a TCP socket the facade never sees and the
extraction ban-list does not forbid, so **mail is the first thing to escape the
kernel plane**, and it is the worst possible candidate for an exception because
it is the channel that reaches people.

Spec 030 §3.5 already refused this shape of hole for pub/sub, in a sentence that
applies verbatim: "a governed deployment whose messages leave unadjudicated has
an ungoverned channel, and the whole kernel plane would be arguable."

So the kernel gains `smtp.egress`, in the same shape as `http.egress`:

| | HTTP | SMTP |
|---|---|---|
| adjudicated as | `http.egress` | `smtp.egress` |
| constraining attribute | `domain` | `host` |
| sole permitted module | `backend/kernel/egress.ts` | `backend/mail/transport.ts` |
| enforced by | extraction ban-list (bare `fetch`) | extraction ban-list (raw socket / mailer import) |
| capability | `cap.egress.rauthy` | `cap.smtp.<name>` |

Provider HTTPS APIs (Resend, Postmark, SES) need none of this and keep using
`governedFetch`. The new kind exists for the self-hosted case, which is this
substrate's primary one: an association with an internal relay and no SaaS
account.

## A notice is a resource, not a function call

Sending is the one operation here that is **not idempotent**. Everything else
reconciles: `admit` normalizes to what is stored and returns without a revision
(spec 034 §3.3), which is what lets spec 036's controller reconcile a membership
a hundred times and raise one invoice. A mail call reconciled a hundred times
sends a hundred emails, and the recipient is a person who now distrusts the
software.

So delivery is reconciliation over a `mailNotice` kind, and idempotence comes
from where it always comes from here: **the name**, derived from what the notice
is about (`dues-reminder-<invoice-name>`) and never from a clock or a counter.
Raising the same notice twice raises one.

Retry is a status with backoff rather than a queue, and a notice that exhausts
its attempts stays visible as `failed`. A notice that gave up silently is worse
than one never raised, because the treasurer believes the member was told.

This is also the "never block a request on a relay" position, delivered without a
second piece of infrastructure. **Redis plus a job runner would buy retry
semantics the control plane already has** (`OUTBOX_TABLE`, written in the same
`txn` as the resource row, drained by a leased controller) **and would cost the
one container and one volume the whole architecture is organized around.**

## The application's mail credentials are a separate surface

The decision most likely to look like an oversight, so the spec states it first.

Spec 026's mapping runs inside the rauthy subshell for exactly one reason: to
keep the IdP's mail credentials out of the application process. Application mail
needs credentials **in** that process. Pointing it at `ENRAHITU_SMTP_*` would
therefore dismantle the invariant 026 was written to establish, and would do it
quietly, since those variables would simply stop being subshell-scoped.

The app gets `ENRAHITU_MAIL_*`. An operator may point both at one relay and most
will: that is configuration duplication, which is cheap, where sharing a variable
would be privilege duplication, which is not.

## Templates: chassis defaults, `app/` overrides

Deliberately the opposite of the manifest overlay's refuse-the-collision rule,
and the asymmetry is the interesting part. A silently overridden **capability** is
a widened security ceiling that reads like a chassis decision. A silently
overridden **template** is an association choosing the wording of its own dues
notice, which is the entire point of the spec 035 boundary.

The cost is named rather than hidden: an improved default cannot reach a
deployment that overrode it, and cannot, because reaching it would mean
overwriting somebody's letterhead.

One constraint on the rendering engine, and only one: it must not put React in
the backend, which today has none.

## Also

`ENRAHITU_MAIL_TRANSPORT=none` is the default and is not a testing convenience. A
deployment with no mail configured still raises notices and leaves them
`pending`, visibly, so turning mail on later delivers the backlog rather than
discovering six months of reminders evaporated.

Cross-references corrected in the two specs that pointed at the wrong owner: 026
§5 now names 037 rather than deferring to spec 030's territory, and 036 §5
distinguishes the two channels and keeps scheduling with the domain, since 037
delivers what the domain raises rather than deciding when.

Registry compiles 38 specs, 0 warnings; `lint` 0 errors; index fresh; 288 tests
still passing; typecheck clean. No code changes: `implementation: pending`.

title: feat(026,033): IdP mail delivery, and a catcher that makes it verifiable
body:
The second user becomes possible. rauthy shipped inside the image with no mail
configuration anywhere, so password reset, email verification, registration and
invitation were all silently inert: the bootstrapped admin was the only account
anyone could ever sign in as, and a forgotten password on it was terminal.

The entrypoint now passes an `ENRAHITU_SMTP_*` operator surface into rauthy's own
`SMTP_*` names, scoped to the rauthy subshell so mail credentials never reach the
app process. `docker/smtp.env.example` documents every mapped variable with a
worked authenticated relay and a worked unauthenticated internal one.

## The prefix did not do what the spec claimed for it

Visible only once the code existed. Mapping `ENRAHITU_SMTP_*` onto `SMTP_*` stops
an ambient variable being **mapped** and does nothing at all about it being
**inherited**. rauthy reads `SMTP_URL` from its environment either way, so an
orchestrator exporting a shared `SMTP_*` for some other workload would have
configured this IdP's mail exactly as before, silently, which is the precise
outcome §3.1 said the prefix prevented.

The entrypoint therefore **scrubs `SMTP_*` before either process starts** and only
then maps. That is what makes `ENRAHITU_SMTP_*` the sole surface that can
configure mail here. The scrub runs at top level rather than in the subshell so
the app process is covered too: an ambient `SMTP_PASSWORD` is a credential, and
the app has no more business holding one it inherited than one we handed it.

Spec 026 §3.1 carries the corrected reasoning rather than quietly dropping the
claim.

## Removing the concession

§3.3 previously conceded that "the delivery path is not exercised by CI: a live
SMTP server is external state." That was avoidable, and removing it is the larger
half of this change.

The dev topology gains **Mailpit**, which converts the external state into
internal state: the same move spec 033 made for the whole dev loop, for the same
reason, that anything only reproducible on CI is a defect you meet late. Chosen
over MailHog (unmaintained), Maildev and Inbucket on three properties:

| property | why it decided |
|---|---|
| single static binary | the shape this topology already uses for rauthy |
| MIT licensed | clears spec 001 §4.7's permissive posture |
| REST API | a test can assert on what was delivered, not a human reading a UI |

It appears in the dev compose file and nowhere else. The packaged image takes a
real relay through the same variables, so the tiers differ in **which relay is
configured, not in whether the code path runs**.

## Verified in the running topology

- rauthy logs a real SMTP connection: `Successfully connected to INSECURE SMTP relay smtp_url="mailpit" port=1025`
- a password reset requested through the app's own origin is **delivered**, `From: enrahitu-dev@localhost`, which is the configured `ENRAHITU_SMTP_FROM` and not a rauthy default, so the passthrough carried it
- the message body carries a reset link on the app's own origin
  (`http://localhost:4000/auth/v1/users/.../reset/...`). That was not the point
  and is worth keeping: **spec 005's same-origin invariant holds through the mail
  path**, which nothing previously checked.

Still not automated: a browser following that link to a completed password
change. The pieces exist for it now (spec 017's Playwright harness plus the REST
API, which is why the REST API decided the tool choice) and it lands with the
next change to that harness. rauthy guards the reset request with a proof of
work, so the test has to solve one; that is a harness concern rather than a
delivery one, and §3.3 names it so the seam is not mistaken for an oversight.

## Tests

They lift the real functions out of the shipped script, so they break when
someone edits the entrypoint rather than when someone edits a copy of it: the
mapping, an unset variable staying absent rather than empty, an ambient `SMTP_*`
being removed, an `ENRAHITU_SMTP_*` winning over one, no `SMTP_*` reaching the app
process, placement of both calls, and the first-boot notice on both sides of its
condition.

288 tests (9 new). Local gate: typecheck clean, `lint` 0 errors, `compile` 37
specs 0 warnings, `index` fresh, `check:model` / `check:manifest` /
`check:chassis` / `check:infra` / `check:licenses` all fresh, `bash -n` and
shellcheck clean on the entrypoint.

## One trap recorded

`docker/entrypoint.sh` and `docker/first-boot.mjs` are COPIED into the dev image
rather than read from the mount, deliberately, so a container still boots when
the tree is mid-edit. The watch loop does not pick them up and a change to either
needs `docker compose up -d --build`. This cost a confusing round trip here and
is now in spec 033 so it costs the next person none.

Specs 007 and 025 take authoring amendments for the files they own rather than
being waived: the entrypoint's environment discipline, and the first-boot suite
widening on the boundary 025 already drew for spec 033's restore guard.

Nothing else is waived: docker/entrypoint.sh, docker/first-boot.mjs and their test suites take authoring amendments to specs 007 and 025.

title: feat(036,015): backdating a payment, and a divergence that was not one
body:
A treasurer can record the cheque that arrived last week on the day it arrived.
`POST /api/dues/:name/paid` takes an optional `paidOn`, and the member and dues
screens carry a date field that means today when left empty.

## The gap was a finding that turns out to be false

Spec 036 shipped `recordPayment` with no backdating, on a recorded finding that
the query-parameter form "parsed on the host and failed in the container against
the same toolchain version". **There is no such divergence**, and this matters
beyond one field: no endpoint in the tree had ever used `Query<T>`, so a
container-side failure of it would have been an undiscovered constraint on the
whole API surface.

At the same toolchain version (0.4.0, unchanged since spec 032 landed and
therefore across the whole life of this domain), reproduced rather than argued:

| | host | container |
|---|---|---|
| build with `Query<string>` | passes | passes, from a cleaned `.encore/build` |
| app metadata | 24623 bytes | 24623 bytes, carrying `query:"paidOn,optional"` |
| runtime decode, value sent | n/a | 200, decodes correctly |
| runtime decode, bare POST | n/a | 200 |

## What was real

The reason the field cannot go in the body reproduces exactly as recorded. Probed
with two throwaway endpoints in the running container, one carrying the value as
a query parameter and one as an optional body field:

| shape | bare `POST` (no body) | with value |
|---|---|---|
| optional **body** field | **400** `unable to decode request body: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0` | 200 |
| optional **query** param | **200** | 200 |

One optional body field makes the body mandatory, so the common case ("paid
today") breaks. That is why `paidOn` rides the query string.

## Why the wrong conclusion was available

The domain was built during the window when the dev loop had the two defects
PR #46 fixed: a failed parse left the watcher believing a build was still running,
so it stopped rebuilding and went on serving the previous bundle, and every
restart left a stale state-machine lock that made the restarted app answer 500 on
`/readyz`. Both present as "the host is fine and the container is broken," and
neither has anything to do with the code being edited.

Spec 036 §3.9 records the general form, because the trap is still available: a
host/container divergence claimed while the dev loop is unsound is a claim about
the dev loop, and an observation whose mechanism cannot be named is a symptom
rather than a constraint.

## The rule

A pure function next to the calendar arithmetic, so its branches are reachable
without a node. Absent, the day is today. Present, it must be a day that exists
and must not be in the future, refused naming the field: a receipt dated forward
records nothing that happened, and the ordinary way to produce one is a typo in
the year. The clock is read once and passed in, so the default and the comparison
cannot straddle midnight.

Backdating cannot move a term. §3.7 reads the invoice's state and its `periodEnd`
and never `paidOn`, so the day money arrived is bookkeeping and never an input to
what it bought.

Spec 015 takes the screen half, following the pattern PR #44 set when these
screens arrived: empty means today and is never sent (forwarding an untouched
date input would put `?paidOn=` on the wire and earn a 400 for the ordinary
case); the picker's ceiling is UTC today rather than the browser's local day,
which east of UTC would offer a day the server refuses; and the field sits inline
on the row, so payment received today stays one click.

## Verified against the running container

Authenticated as an operator through the mock driver, against the real endpoint:

- bare `POST` and a valid backdate both reach the store (404 on a name that does
  not exist, not a decode failure)
- a future day and a day that does not exist are refused 400 naming the field
- a real invoice backdated to `2026-01-15` stored that day, and its membership
  renewed to `2026-01-01` through `2027-01-01` from the invoice's own period,
  confirming the payment date did not move the term

`lint` 0 errors, `compile` 37 specs 0 warnings, `index` fresh, `check:model` /
`check:manifest` / `check:chassis` / `check:infra` / `check:licenses` all fresh.
