They carry no authored intent, and editing spec 035, 006 or 019 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration would be amending an owning spec to satisfy a refresh, which .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids. The frontend source changes are not waived: spec 015 carries an authoring amendment, following PR #44.

title: fix(002,033): the dev loop stops eating itself
body:
## Summary

Two defects found by using the N=1 container for a full session. One is a development papercut; the other is not a development problem at all.

**The hiqlite state-machine lock is never released.** hiqlite writes `<data>/state_machine/lock` when the SQLite state machine opens and removes it in exactly one place, `Client::shutdown()`. The addon exposes no `shutdown()` and nothing here has ever called it, so the lock survives SIGTERM, a clean `docker compose stop`, and every rebuild of the watch loop. The next start panics with "Node did not shut down gracefully - needs manual interaction" and the store stays shut until a human deletes a file inside the container.

Spec 036 §3.2 keeps a store that will not open from taking down `/healthz` and the login flow, which is correct and also excellent camouflage: the symptom is `/readyz` 500 on a container whose liveness probe is green, and it survives every restart. Under the watch loop it lands on the **first edit of a session**; under a restart policy it lands after any hard kill and never clears. The container log for this session carries the panic after nearly every rebuild, for hours.

`backend/hiq/lock.ts` supplies what a zero-byte lock naming no owner cannot. Each node start records its owner (pid, host) at the data-dir root before `init()`, and a start that finds a lock clears it only when it can prove that owner is dead. A lock a live process still holds is left alone, so hiqlite's panic stays correct for the case it exists for. The check never throws: it runs at module load, where an exception is not a failed recovery but a failed import, and would make an unopenable store strictly worse than before.

Releasing the lock on the way down is the real fix and lives in the addon. Spec 032's implementation record files it as the decision the interface contract never made, with the two details that work needs: `shutdown()` deliberately delays about ten seconds, and at N=3 it is what lets a node leave the cluster cleanly. Recovery is still needed afterwards, because SIGKILL and the OOM killer never call anything.

**The watch loop went deaf.** `stopApp` waited on an `exit` event from a process that had already exited, so the promise never settled, `building` stayed true, and every later change took the early return: the watcher alive, silent, and useless, recoverable only by restarting the container. It now recognizes an already-exited process, settles on an absolute deadline, and tracks the child by identity, so an exit by signal or with status 0 drops the reference. inotify also proved undependable across the bind mount, so a content-hash fingerprint of the same files is now the floor under `fs.watch` (`ENRAHITU_WATCH_POLL_MS`, default 1000).

## Testing

- `npm test`: 274 passed, 12 skipped (14 new, covering every branch of the reclaim decision including the never-throws guarantee).
- `npm run typecheck`, `check:manifest`, `check:infra`, `check:chassis`, `check:model`, `check:licenses`: clean.
- `spec-spine compile` / `lint --fail-on-warn` / `index check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings, index fresh.
- Verified against the running N=1 container rather than argued: a volume carrying a legacy lock recovered through the `no-owner-record` path, the next restart through `owner-gone`, and three consecutive watch-loop rebuilds each logged the reclaim and then `members: runtime started`. Before this change, the first rebuild of a session ended the domain until a human intervened.

title: feat(023,027): the schema verb, so a deployment can apply its control plane
body:
## Why

Nothing in the tree applied `CONTROL_PLANE_MIGRATIONS` to a deployed container. The control plane's tables existed in tests and nowhere else, so spec 036's domain shipped on a schema no deployment had, and every members endpoint correctly answered 503 forever.

This is the other half, deliberately kept out of #44: an operator endpoint and a primary key have different reversibility profiles and should not share one Decision.

## What

`GET /api/admin/schema` reports the applied version and what is pending. `POST /api/admin/schema/apply` applies it, idempotently. Both behind spec 023 section 3.1's existing gate, unchanged.

## Why an endpoint rather than a script under `scripts/ops/`

Spec 032 section 3.6 settled that migration is a deploy step with one runner and not a boot step, and this does not reopen it. The complication is where the store is: at N=1 the app's embedded hiqlite node holds the volume open, so no second process can reach it while the app runs. The deploy step has to be performed **by** the running app, which is the one process that can.

The operator plane is then the right place for an operator's act. It is authenticated, role-gated, and adjudicated, so the migration lands on the Decision chain naming a principal. A shell script on the host would be none of those.

"One runner by construction" is satisfied by an operator invoking it once.

## The ceiling stays readable

The `admin` service holds `cap.db.state.migrate` and `cap.db.state.read` in the manifest and calls the runner under its own attribution. It does **not** borrow the `state` service's identity through `runAsService`, which would put a capability in the model that the manifest does not show. A readable ceiling is the whole point of spec 021.

`members` deliberately holds no `db.migrate`: a domain service that could migrate is one that could migrate by accident. Asserted.

## The extractor caught a real mistake

The first version imported `CONTROL_PLANE_MIGRATIONS` from the control plane's barrel, and `enrahitu-extract` immediately refused:

```
- service 'admin' uses notify.publish on 'state' (via backend/control/admission.ts) beyond its declared ceiling
- service 'admin' uses db.txn on 'state' (via backend/control/admission.ts) beyond its declared ceiling
```

A barrel import drags every effect reachable through it into the importing service's traced surface. Importing `../control/schema` directly narrows it back to the constant that was wanted. **What a service imports is part of what it claims**, and the model is what noticed.

## No new UI

The dashboard's existing API caller invokes both endpoints under the operator's own session, so the verb is usable the day it lands rather than the day a panel is designed for it.

## Evidence

4 new tests (260 total): reports what is pending before acting, applies under `admin`'s own attribution, applies nothing the second time rather than failing on a constraint, and is denied to a service the manifest does not grant it to. The planner is a pure function in its own module so the decision an operator is about to take is assertable without an Encore build.

Verified end to end in the N=1 container, which is what this PR exists to make possible:

```
GET  /api/admin/schema        {"version":0,"pending":[{"name":"control plane: resources, outbox, watermarks","version":1}]}
POST /api/admin/schema/apply  {"version":1,"applied":[{"name":"control plane: ...","version":1}]}
GET  /api/admin/schema        {"version":1,"pending":[]}
```

Then the domain came up on its own (`members: created the association record`, `members: runtime started`), and the full loop ran against real data: a tier and a member created, a membership enrolled with an already-expired term, the renewal controller raising `ada-individual-2026-07-01` for $45.00 due 2026-07-31 without being asked, and recording payment **on the invoice alone** renewing the membership to 2027-07-01 with nothing calling it. The membership's revision then held steady across repeated passes, which is the quiescence rule spec 034 section 3.3 exists for. Decision chain verified throughout.

Local gate: typecheck clean, 260 tests passing, `lint` 0 errors, `compile` 37 specs 0 warnings, `index check` fresh, `check:model` / `check:manifest` / `check:chassis` / `check:infra` all fresh.

They carry no authored intent, and amending spec 021 or 035 to acknowledge a mechanical regeneration is what .claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md forbids.

title: feat(036): the membership core, the domain the control plane was built for
body:
## Why

Spec 034 built the control plane and spec 035 drew the boundary around it. Both were written for a domain that did not exist yet, and a machine built for a load it has never carried is a hypothesis. This is the load.

It is also the first change in the corpus with a buyer's question attached rather than an architect's. Spec 001 section 4.1 names the reader: a 200-member association with no ops team, who wants to know who is a member, what they owe, and who has lapsed.

**One domain, completely, rather than eleven shallowly.** The questions that break a design are second-order (what happens when a tier is deleted while memberships reference it, when a controller and a person write the same row, when the reconciler runs twice), and they only appear once one domain is finished. The rest land afterwards in the shape this one establishes.

Five kinds registered at runtime with **zero DDL**, which is the property spec 035 section 3.4 promised would make the chassis boundary cheap, spent for the first time.

## Three decisions the domain forced

### The tenant is an operator-chosen slug, guarded by a boot assertion

`ENRAHITU_TENANT`, required in production, `local-dev` outside it, never generated.

The tempting argument for putting the tenant in the key is wrong and spec 036 section 3.2 says so: the chain hashes Decision records in `kernel_decisions`, `verifyChain` reads that table only, so a later backfill could not break it. What a backfill would actually cost is a permanent footnote in the audit story, where historical records name an identity that no longer resolves. Real, permanent, small. The decision rests on the cost comparison instead: carrying the tenant now costs approximately nothing, because `admit` demands one from a tenant-scoped kind and every call site passes one either way.

A generated `org-<hex>` was the first answer and was rejected: it makes the value that seeds every primary key machine-specific, it puts that identity in a file with no admission record so a lost volume silently re-mints it and orphans every surviving row, and opacity buys nothing when fleet-hosting produces separate apps rather than tenants inside one.

**The boot assertion matters more than the choice of identifier.** If the resolved tenant and the stored one disagree, the deployment writes a second invisible dataset alongside the first: silent, compounding, and worse the longer it runs. It refuses to start and names both values. Costs one read of one column.

The narrow claim is written down so it is not over-trusted later: this avoids a permanent translation rule in the audit story. It does not make the app multi-tenant ready.

### Referential integrity is observed, not enforced

A membership names a tier by name and nothing stops the tier being retracted. Admission could refuse the dangling case and deliberately does not: checking a reference inside the admitting transaction is a second store crossing for a guarantee that expires the moment the referent is retracted. The check would pass at write time and the row would dangle an hour later anyway, and enforcement that cannot hold is worse than none because it reads like a guarantee.

So the controller reports it. A membership whose tier is gone gets `status.state = "invalid"` naming the missing tier, visible in the roster. Retracting a tier that memberships use is a legitimate operator act, and the right response is to show what it broke.

### The fencing token is also the human plane's concurrency control

Spec 034 built `fence` for one question: a controller that lost its lease mid-reconcile. The domain asks a second. The renewal controller writes status under its pass token, so the row's mark is non-zero, and an endpoint admitting at the default fence of 0 is refused forever.

The rule is that an endpoint passes the fence it read. Four lines, and it resolves both: a person can always land a write on a controller-written row, and if a controller wrote in between, the mark moved and the endpoint answers 409 rather than silently clobbering. The fence became optimistic concurrency for the human plane at no cost.

## Also here

**`setStatus` (amends spec 034).** Spec 034 section 5 named `status` as "a column a controller writes through the same admission path" and the implementation had no such path: `admit`'s `ON CONFLICT` sets revision, fence, spec, deleted_at and updated_at, never status. So status was readable and unwritable by anything in the tree. Same five steps, minus validation, and the no-op rule extends verbatim because every reconciler here writes status to a kind it also watches.

**A Tenant is the association (amends spec 001 section 5.3).** The word carried three candidates at once: the association, a chapter, a fleet-hosted org. Harmless until it entered a primary key. Chapters are subordinate scopes within one tenant; fleet-hosting produces separate apps.

**Two loops, not one.** A change feed cannot observe the passage of time, and a membership expiring tomorrow is not written tomorrow. The change loop reacts to writes and the sweep reacts to the calendar. They share one lease key, which buys both mutual exclusion and strictly ordered fencing tokens; two keys would produce a steady trickle of meaningless `SupersededError`s.

## Not included, deliberately

**The schema verb.** Nothing applies `CONTROL_PLANE_MIGRATIONS` to a deployed container yet, so every members endpoint answers 503 naming the precondition and the controller waits rather than failing a pass per second. Supplying it is a separate change against specs 023 and 027: an operator endpoint and a primary key have different reversibility profiles and should not share one Decision.

## Evidence

37 new tests (256 total). The pure renewal rule is asserted at every branch of its table without a store, because a renewal rule is a policy a board approves and a policy readable only as a sequence of store calls cannot be reviewed by the people whose policy it is. The rest run against a booted node.

Two assertions are worth naming. Re-admitting an unchanged spec produces no revision and no outbox row, which is what makes a converged controller quiescent. And two tenants reconcile independently through one pass, asserted rather than assumed because `changesSince` carries no tenant predicate and never will: the reconciler's signature is the only thing holding isolation.

Verified in the N=1 container rather than only in tests: the service boots, logs the schema wait once, serves the legible 503 to an authenticated operator, and the SPA renders it as a sentence.

**Running it found two bugs in this change that the tests could not.** The boot path exited the process on any startup failure, so a volume left locked by an unclean shutdown took down `/healthz`, the admin dashboard and the login flow with it, which are exactly what an operator needs when the store will not open; only a tenant mismatch exits now. And the payment action required a request body, because one optional field is enough to make the body mandatory, so a correct `POST .../paid` answered "EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 0".

The SPA half found two more. The membership loaders never refreshed an expired access token, so the first request after the TTL told a signed-in operator they were signed out. Fixing that exposed the sharper one: refresh tokens rotate on use, so two loaders on one route each started a rotation and the second presented a token the first had consumed, burning the session's chain. Rotation is single-flighted now, which is a correctness requirement in shared code rather than an optimization in mine.

Local gate: typecheck clean, 256 tests passing, `lint` 0 errors, `compile` 37 specs 0 warnings, `index check` fresh, `check:model` / `check:manifest` / `check:chassis` / `check:infra` all fresh.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: app-manifest.json, app-model.json, chassis.lock, backend/web/dist/index.html are derived artifacts regenerated by gen:manifest, extract:model, chassis:lock and the SPA build. title: feat(035): the chassis/tree boundary and upgrade mechanics
body:
## Why

Spec 001 section 4.1 says the product "ships as a working application that an organization extends rather than forks". Every word after "extends" is a promise about upgrades, and nothing enforced it.

Before this PR, an organization's only way to add a capability was to edit `app-manifest.json` — a chassis file. The first upgrade would silently discard the grant, and the extension would start failing adjudication with no obvious cause. The promise and the mechanism disagreed, and the mechanism was going to win.

This lands before phase 5 for the reason spec 001 section 5.1 gives: it decides what the application baseline is allowed to contain. A baseline written without a boundary produces a boundary drawn around whatever the baseline happened to do.

## The boundary

**`app/` is the organization's. Everything else is the chassis's.**

One directory, not extension points scattered through the tree. The alternative fails the only test that matters: a reader cannot tell from a path whether an upgrade will overwrite it. One root answers that from the path alone.

The chassis roster is an **inclusion** list, not "everything except `app/`". That is not stylistic. An exclusion list makes a newly added top-level directory chassis-owned by default, so whoever adds one silently takes it away from the organization. An inclusion list makes the same mistake a missing entry that `check:chassis` reports on the next commit.

## Three mechanisms

### The manifest splits

| file | owner | on upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| `app-manifest.chassis.json` | chassis | replaced wholesale |
| `app/manifest.json` | organization | never touched |
| `app-manifest.json` | derived | regenerated |

`gen-manifest.mjs` composes them, `check:manifest` gates it, following `gen-infra-config.mjs` exactly (spec 033 section 3.4).

**The composition refuses rather than merges.** An overlay may add capabilities, services and resources; it may not redefine a chassis one, and the collision is an error rather than last-writer-wins. Precedence is the wrong tool: a silently overridden capability is a widened ceiling that reads, in the composed file, exactly like a chassis decision. An organization that needs different chassis grants is asking for a chassis change, and that conversation should happen out loud.

One exception, without which the boundary would be useless: an overlay may **add** capabilities to a chassis service. Additive, visible in the output, and the only way an organization's kind can be reconciled by a chassis controller.

### The chassis lock

`chassis.lock`, a sha256 per chassis file, committed and shipped inside the artifact.

**Why a lock rather than a diff against upstream.** A diff needs a remote, a fetch, and shared history. A stamped app may have none: spec 012's provenance records where it came from, not a live link back. A hash list answers the question offline, which is the same reason `package-lock.json` exists rather than resolving the registry every time.

### The preflight

```
$ npm run upgrade:preflight
[chassis-lock] 225 chassis file(s) unmodified: an upgrade replaces these silently.

[chassis-lock] An upgrade would DISCARD the following local changes:
    M backend/health/api.ts

[chassis-lock] Each one is a fork of the chassis at that path. For every file above, either
    - move the change into app/, where an upgrade never reaches, or
    - propose it upstream, so the chassis carries it and every deployment gets it, or
    - accept losing it, and re-apply after the upgrade.
[chassis-lock] Nothing under app/ was examined; that directory is yours.
```

Exits nonzero on modified or removed. Files added inside a chassis root are reported but are not a hazard: they are the organization's until the chassis ships one at the same path, and that collision surfaces as `modified` on the next lock.

## Phase 3 is what makes this cheap

An extension is a kind registered at runtime, a controller, a service with its own grants. No migration, no schema change, no chassis file touched. That property had to be true before phase 5 could ship a domain without freezing it.

## The one unsolved case, named rather than hidden

**Frontend extension.** Adding a route still means editing a chassis file under `frontend/`. The router would need a registration seam equivalent to the kind registry, and designing one on the way past would be designing it badly. Spec 035 section 5 states it.

Also out of scope, with reasons: applying an upgrade (this makes consequences visible before the fact; performing the replacement is the factory's and an operational verb's), and moving the composition into the extractor — Fork 4 decided the seam is the model, so it belongs in `@statecrafting/toolchain` eventually, but the composition rules are new and a wrong rule set is far cheaper to change here than in a published package three repositories consume.

## Evidence

12 new tests, asserting the properties each mechanism exists to guarantee rather than its happy path: the composer must **refuse** the collisions that widen a ceiling invisibly, and the preflight must **notice** the edits an upgrade would discard. A composer that merges quietly and a preflight that reports nothing both look like success.

End to end: edited a chassis file, observed the report and the nonzero exit, reverted, observed safe.

Full suite 219 passing. Local gate: `compile` 36 specs 0 warnings, `lint --fail-on-warn` clean, `index check` fresh, `couple` 17 paths no drift, `check:model`/`check:manifest`/`check:chassis` all fresh.

title: feat(034): the control plane: kinds, admission, watch, controllers, audit
body:
> Reopened against `main` (the original #41 was auto-closed when its stacked base branch merged and was deleted).

## What

Phase 3 of the pivot, and the layer spec 001 calls "application code holds intent and reconciliation": `backend/control/`, plus spec 034.

Typed, tenant-scoped resources admitted through the kernel onto the state layer; a change feed ordered by one global revision; leased, fenced, watermarked reconcile loops; and an admission record on the Decision chain.

It is deliberately the shape Kubernetes made ordinary, and that is not imitation. It is the only shape that survives the two properties this substrate actually has, both recorded in spec 032 rather than chosen here: **a lease that expires in ten seconds whether or not its holder is finished**, and **a notify that is a hint rather than a delivery**. Any design in which a change is applied once and assumed to have taken is wrong under either one.

## Two defects that only a running node produced

Spec 001 section 5.1 says phase 3 is "back-written from what real nodes did, not designed ahead of them". These are what that bought.

### hiqlite binds parameters positionally and ignores the number

```sql
-- params: ["A", "B"]
SELECT * FROM t WHERE b = $2 AND a = $1   -- binds b := "A", a := "B"
```

No error, no warning. A `SELECT` returns the wrong rows, an `UPDATE` reports zero rows affected, an `INSERT ... SELECT` inserts nothing. It surfaced as two silently empty tables and a soft-delete tombstone that never appeared, and none of the three symptoms pointed at parameter binding; isolating it took a dedicated probe script.

Statements whose numbers happen to ascend by first appearance work correctly, which is most hand-written SQL. That is what makes it dangerous: it works until someone writes a `WHERE` clause in a different order than the `SET` clause.

`backend/state/placeholders.ts` now checks every statement crossing the facade and throws naming it. Filed upstream as statecrafting#16 with a suggested fix.

### An admission that changes nothing must not produce a revision

Found by a test that timed out, not by review. A controller that writes a resource it also watches sees its own write as a new revision, reconciles again, writes again, and spins until its lease expires. Admission now returns the stored resource unchanged when the normalized spec and fence both match: no write, no outbox row, no notify.

This is also why a kind's validator returns a normalized value rather than a verdict. Two inputs that normalize to the same resource must compare equal, or a converged controller never becomes quiescent.

## The revision, and why deletes are soft

`revision` is one monotonic sequence across every resource, computed as `MAX(revision) + 1` **inside** the admitting transaction.

The obvious alternative is wrong. Bumping a sequence row first and writing with the value it returned takes two raft operations, so two writers interleave: W1 takes revision 5, W2 takes 6, W2 commits, W1 commits. A watcher polling between those commits sees 6, advances past 5, and never sees W1's write. Computing inside the transaction makes revision order and commit order the same order, because raft serializes the transactions, and that identity is the entire basis of the watermark's correctness.

So deletes are soft: a hard delete could lower `MAX(revision)` and hand a later write a revision a watcher had already passed. A tombstone is also what a watcher needs to observe a deletion at all, since a row that vanishes is indistinguishable from one it never saw.

## Grants

`control` is `role: library` and holds six: `db.read`/`db.write`/`db.txn` on `state`, `lock.acquire`, and both notify capabilities.

It does **not** hold `db.migrate` (schema is the `state` service's, which is why `CONTROL_PLANE_MIGRATIONS` is exported as data for the migration runner) and it does not hold the backup grants (bracketing a risky operation with a backup is an operator verb, and a controller that could take backups on its own schedule can fill a volume). `control.test.ts` asserts the migrate denial rather than assuming it.

That leaves exactly one of spec 032's nine declared capabilities still granted to nobody: `bucket.write` on `state-backups`, whose holder is spec 027's verb.

## Deliberately not here

- **The association domain.** Phase 5. This is the machinery; members, tiers, dues and events are kinds registered on it.
- **The Decision chain's migration to hiqlite**, its hot window and segment sealing (spec 032 sections 3.7 and 3.9). Spec 024's territory, and a distinct change with its own risk.
- **Per-kind capability grants.** The kernel's narrowing axis for `db.*` is the `tables` constraint and every kind shares one table, so the axis buys nothing as the schema stands; making a kind its own capability resource is a contract question about the model. Spec 020 section 3.4 already carries per-verb and per-table attribution as a named v0.2 extension, and this belongs on that list.
- **HTTP endpoints.** The domain publishes them, each under its own service's attribution, so a member-facing handler cannot borrow the control plane's ceiling by calling through it.

## Evidence

19 new tests, all against a booted node, covering the ten acceptance items in spec 034 section 4. Full suite 207 passing.

Local gate: `compile` 35 specs 0 warnings, `lint --fail-on-warn` clean, `index check` fresh, `couple` 17 paths no drift, `check:model` fresh.

title: feat(032): the state layer facade, and phase 2 closes
body:
## What

`backend/state/`, the governed facade over `@statecrafting/hiqlite-native` 0.2.0. Spec 032 moves to `implementation: complete`, which closes phase 2 of the pivot.

Five modules behind one barrel, split the way the contract's section 4 groups the surface: `sql` (3.1, 3.3), `watch` (3.2), `lease` (3.4), `backup` (3.8), and `migrate` (3.6, the only one with policy of its own, because the addon deliberately exposes no migrate entry point).

## Three things the contract left to the facade

**The watch pump.** The addon exposes `listenNext()`, one event per call, and hiqlite's bus delivers each event to a single awaiter. Two concurrent `listenNext()` callers would steal events from each other and each see an arbitrary half of the stream, so fan-out cannot be the caller's problem: one pump per process dispatches to every handler. One consequence, stated because it is invisible otherwise: `listenNext()` cannot be cancelled, so when the last handler unsubscribes the pump consumes and discards one further event before exiting. Harmless under the watermark rule; not harmless under any design that treats delivery as authoritative.

**`backup` adjudicates as `bucket.write`.** The kernel's vocabulary is a fixed 28 kinds (spec 020 section 3.3) and boot refuses a model declaring one it does not know, so a `backup.*` kind would need a kernel-native release before this facade could exist at all. It is not needed either: a backup genuinely is an object-store write of the database, and `bucket.write` is classified non-read, so it fails closed at `read-only` trust.

**Table narrowing is opt-in.** The kernel checks a `tables` constraint against a request's `table`/`tables` attribute, so a grant declaring tables denies any call that does not name them. The facade cannot infer them without parsing SQL, which would make the security boundary depend on a parser.

## What holds these grants

A `state` service, `role: library`, with `db.migrate` and `db.read` on `state` and nothing else. It owns the schema, so it may change the schema and read what version it is at; it cannot write a row, take a lease, publish a notify, or touch a backup.

The other seven capabilities are declared in the model and granted to no service. `backend/state/state.test.ts` asserts each one denies **in fact**, so the withholding is evidence rather than intention. They land on phase 3's control plane, the first thing with a reason to hold them.

## What moved elsewhere to make it possible

- **statecrafting toolchain 0.4.0** (its spec 002 amendment, PR #15): the extract surface wired exactly one governed facade over the addon in by name, so every file here tripped the `raw-hiq-init-import` ban. That ban is now a path-prefix rule over two facades, split by raft group, plus `STATE_KINDS`.
- **`contracts/app-model.schema.json`** had no `hiqlite` engine (spec 020 amendment).
- **`resources.buckets`** existed in the schema and had never been populated; `state-backups` is its first entry (spec 021 amendment).

Both consumer-side gaps were found by the extractor refusing the model, which is the schema doing its job.

## Division of evidence

The addon's `sanity-state.mjs` proves the surface (txn atomicity, the query/queryConsistent split, fence monotonicity and durability, lease behavior) on all three platforms, under statecrafting's new build gate (its spec 007). This suite proves what is only true on this side: that every crossing adjudicates against the right kind and resource, and the migration runner's ordering, duplicate refusal, and idempotence. Both run against a real booted node; neither repeats the other.

## Verification

Written and proven first against a locally built addon patched into `node_modules`, then re-verified against what npm actually serves: `npm ci` from a clean tree, then typecheck, license gate, model extraction and the full suite, all green against the published artifacts. The only model movement from the toolchain bump is the extractor's own version stamp and the hashes derived from it, with no capability, service or resource drift, which is the evidence that 0.4.0's extract change did what it claimed and nothing else.

Local gate: `compile` 34 specs 0 warnings, `lint --fail-on-warn` clean, `index check` fresh, `couple` 16 paths no drift, `check:model` fresh, `check:infra` fresh, `check:licenses` clean.

title: docs(032,001): record the four contract corrections the addon forced
body:
Phase 2 landed as `@statecrafting/hiqlite-native` 0.2.0 (statecrafting spec 003, PR #13): nine functions became twenty-one, verified against a running node and against this repo's full suite with the addon patched into `node_modules`.

Building it corrected spec 032 in four places. Recording them here as well as upstream, because spec 032 is the document read **during** the work, and a contract that quietly disagrees with its implementation is worse than one that is wrong out loud.

## The sharpest correction

§3.4 reasoned that hiqlite's lock id is the raft `log_id`, monotonically increasing across the cache group, and therefore "already a valid fencing token" that is "free".

The first half is true. The second is not: `hiqlite::Lock` keeps `id` in a private field with **no accessor**, so the token cannot be obtained through the public API at all.

The replacement is better rather than a workaround. The token is now a monotonic counter in the **SQLite** group, bumped by an upsert with `RETURNING` in one round trip. Lock state lives in the **cache** group, which is not durable and does not survive a full cluster restart, and **a fencing token that resets is not a fencing token**. The fence is now durable, and it lives in the same group as the writes it guards, so the fence and the write commit in one `txn`. The `WHERE fence <= :token` predicate this spec specifies is unchanged.

## The other three

**The lock handle must be parked Rust-side.** `hiqlite::Lock` releases on `Drop`, asynchronously, and JavaScript has no deterministic drop. Without holding it, the lock would release the instant `lock()` returned, so the lease would be a **silent no-op** rather than a short one.

**The notify envelope had to become a concrete struct.** hiqlite serializes bus events with bincode, which cannot decode a free-form JSON value (`Serde(AnyNotSupported)`). That turned out to be what this spec wanted anyway: with fixed fields, a caller **cannot** smuggle a payload onto the cache raft group, so §3.2's key-only decision is now enforced structurally instead of by discipline.

**`backup` makes encryption keys mandatory at boot.** It pulls hiqlite's `s3` feature, which makes `NodeConfig.enc_keys` required, so the node refuses to start without them. That is a boot-contract change this spec did not state. Resolved by taking the same `ENC_KEYS` format rauthy already uses, so a deployment custodies **one** key set for both hiqlite instances: backups are encrypted with them, a tenant that loses them holds unrecoverable ciphertext, and two independent custodies double that exposure for no benefit.

## What did not change

All four decisions that concluded "no new primitive" held. `txn` plus a unique index is still the CAS, and spec 024's retry loop carries over with no change to its assertions. A monotonic column inside the transaction is still the revision sequence. Migrations remain DDL through `txn` guarded by a version table, with no addon entry point. Restore stays outside the addon.

One addition to §4: `executeReturning`. `execute` alone cannot express an upsert that reports the value it settled on, which is exactly what the fence needs, and following a write with a separate read would read through a different consistency path than the one that wrote.

## Spec 032 stays `pending`, deliberately

The contract is settled and the surface is built and proven. What is unbuilt is **this repo's** territory: `backend/state/`, the governed facade application code will actually call. It cannot be written before 0.2.0 is published, because it must compile against the published addon, and a facade calling `query` today fails this repo's own typecheck against 0.1.0.

The index gate refused `implementation: complete` on exactly that ground and was right to. Rounding it up would have been the kind of quiet inaccuracy this corpus exists to prevent.

## Gate

compile 34 / 0 warnings, index 34 mappings / 0 diagnostics, lint 0/0/0, index fresh, couple OK, typecheck clean, 181 tests across 20 files.

title: feat(033): the docker dev topology, watch loop, infra generator, restore guard
body:
Phase 1b of the pivot, second part. Development is now docker-only, and the N=1 dev topology **is** the N=1 deployment topology rather than a parallel arrangement that resembles it.

## What landed

**`docker/compose.yml` + `Dockerfile.dev`** — one container, one volume, one command. rauthy on loopback, the app on the published port, both supervised by the **same `entrypoint.sh` the packaged image uses**, branching on `ENRAHITU_DEV` for exactly one thing: whether the app process is the watch loop or the built bundle.

One supervisor, not two, and that is the load-bearing decision here. The trap handling is spec 007's hardest-won behavior: without it rauthy's embedded hiqlite keeps its WAL and state-machine lock files, the next boot is unclean, and it can escalate into a crash loop. A second entrypoint would be a second place for that to regress.

**`scripts/dev-watch.mjs`** — the backend had no watch at all. The frontend had Vite HMR and the backend had nothing, which was tolerable while `npm run dev` was a process a developer restarted by hand, and stops being tolerable once it is in a container.

**`scripts/gen-infra-config.mjs`** — `infra.config.json` and `infra.config.dev.json` were hand-maintained twins that must agree, with nothing making them agree, and spec 030 adds a third. Now generated from one source with a CI drift gate. It reproduces the previously hand-written files **byte for byte**, so adopting it is a diff of zero rather than a reformat that has to be read to be trusted.

**The restore guard** — `HQL_BACKUP_RESTORE` is applied by hiqlite at boot before the raft node starts, and rauthy's own config documents "remove the value after the restart". Left set in a container with a restart policy it re-applies on **every** restart and discards everything written since: a crash loop becomes silent, repeated data loss, and the operator sees a container restarting rather than one deleting. Designed out rather than documented around, via a marker on the volume plus a `restore.env` handshake mirroring `secrets.env` (a separate process cannot unset a variable in the entrypoint's shell). A *different* identifier is a new restore and is honoured. 7 tests.

## Verified by booting it, which found four defects

Two were in code this change added; two were latent in `entrypoint.sh`, waiting for the first caller that was not the packaged image.

1. **rauthy panics without CA certificates.** `node:24-trixie-slim` ships none, and rauthy builds a `reqwest` client during `init_static_vars`, so it aborts before logging anything of its own. The only visible symptom under the die-together supervisor was "rauthy exited during startup". `Dockerfile.base` already installed them; the dev image did not, and the fact that one file knew and the other did not is exactly the duplication this spec is reducing.
2. **A named volume mounted at `node_modules` initializes root-owned.** Docker seeds it from whatever the image has at that path and creates it root-owned when the path is absent, so the first-run `npm ci` died with `EACCES`. Same problem and same fix as the `/data` ownership the packaged image needs.
3. **`entrypoint.sh` hardcoded `NODE_ENV=production` and `AUTH_DRIVER=rauthy`**, clobbering whatever the topology asked for. `npm ci` then omitted devDependencies, so the build toolchain was absent and the watch loop could not compile; and the mock driver was disabled, leaving a dev container with no way to sign in. Neither symptom pointed anywhere near its cause. Both now use the `${VAR:-…}` idiom that `ENRAHITU_METRICS_TOKEN` and `ENRAHITU_LEDGER_URL` already use three lines below them, so the packaged image lands on identical values.
4. **The watch loop did not set the runtime environment.** A compiled bundle is not self-contained: it needs `ENCORE_RUNTIME_LIB`, the parse step's app metadata, and an infra config with hosted services and gateways merged in.

None of these would have been caught by a compose file that was written, reviewed, and committed without being run.

## Observed against the live topology

From an empty volume: first-boot provisions, rauthy bootstraps and answers on loopback, the container installs its own `node_modules`, the watch loop builds, the app serves.

```
/healthz            200
/readyz             200
/hiq/health         200  {"status":"ok"}      <- the addon, up in-process
/api/v1/auth/status 200  {"drivers":["mock","rauthy"]}
/metrics            401                        <- unauthenticated, spec 025
/auth/v1/.well-known/openid-configuration  200 <- rauthy through the APP's origin
```

That last line is spec 005's same-origin invariant holding in the dev topology, which is the thing the old split loop could never demonstrate locally.

Editing `backend/health/api.ts` produced `rebuilding: backend/health/api.ts` and the app came back serving with no intervention.

## Still open, and stated rather than quietly left

The `compose.dev.yml` retirement (§3.3) is described but not executed: spec 017's Playwright suite still starts it via `npm run dev:idp`, and moving that suite onto the compose topology is its own change. Until then both files exist, which is the duplication this spec exists to remove. Spec 033 stays `implementation: in-progress` for that reason.

title: feat(033): the app-level test harness; close spec 025
body:
Phase 1b of the pivot (spec 001 §5.1), first part.

Every test in this repo was either a pure module test or a subprocess test of a shell script. Neither can answer **"does the running gateway refuse this request?"**, which is the only question that matters for a surface a stranger can reach. Spec 025 shipped four acceptance items it could not prove for exactly that reason, and said so rather than pretending otherwise.

## The harness

`testing/app-harness.ts` boots `.encore/build/combined/combined/main.mjs`: the same bundle the dev runner runs and the container runs, under a throwaway data directory with freshly minted RS256 keys and OS-allocated ports. Requests go over real HTTP through the real gateway, so middleware, the auth handler, the kernel, and the Encore router are all in the path. Nothing is stubbed.

It carries a cookie jar, because the session is httpOnly cookies (spec 004) and `fetch` does not persist them. Without one it could only ever test the unauthenticated surface, which is half the point.

## Three things building it found

**Vitest's environment breaks the child.** The runner sets `NODE_ENV=test` and a family of `VITEST_*` markers; inherited, they put the Encore runtime in test mode, where it never opens its API listener. The symptom is a boot that logs nothing and times out, which reads like a hung application rather than a misconfigured one.

**`NODE_ENV=development` is the only correct default.** `test` is the trap above; `production` disables the mock auth driver (`isMockEnabled()` is `!env.isProduction`), leaving the harness unable to hold a session. Both wrong answers fail in ways that look like application bugs.

That second one turned into coverage rather than just a comment: an instance booted with `NODE_ENV=production` now proves the mock driver is absent and mints no session. `isMockEnabled()` is one line, and a regression inverting it would hand any visitor an admin session by visiting a URL. That is the same class of defect the spec 025 exposure review found elsewhere, and until now nothing asserted it.

**`encore.dev` had drifted from the runtime.** The manifest declared `^1.57.9`, npm resolved 1.57.12, and the toolchain's napi runtime is v1.57.9. The runtime prints a version-mismatch warning on every boot saying this "may cause unexpected behaviour" and continues anyway. Nothing in the repo booted the bundle against the runtime, so nobody read it: the dev runner prints it to a terminal a developer is not watching, and no test started the app at all. Now pinned exactly, because a caret range across a napi ABI boundary is a floating mismatch waiting to happen rather than a convenience.

## Why the harness sits at the repo root

The extraction gate refused it under `backend/`, correctly. The usage walk treats every non-`.test.ts` file there as application code and forbids bare `fetch()`, because ungoverned egress from a service is exactly what `backend/kernel/egress.ts` exists to prevent.

A harness whose entire job is to make HTTP requests at the application from outside is not application code. Putting it under `backend/` would have forced a choice between weakening that ban and misdescribing the file. At the root, the ban and the truth agree. `e2e/` (spec 017) is the existing precedent, and spec 019 already reserves the root for what is not an Encore.ts concern.

This is the second time in this pivot that the kernel plane has refused a design and been right; the first was `apiRateLimit` on the `hiq` service in spec 025.

## Spec 025 closes, and the four items resolve two different ways

**Item 6 is proved.** `/metrics` returns 401 unauthenticated, 401 for a wrong bearer, and 200 with Prometheus exposition format for the right one, against a real gateway with a token provisioned the way first-boot provisions one.

**Items 1 and 4 are superseded, not completed.** They asked for proof that an unauthenticated `POST /hiq/kv` is refused and that a non-`demo:` key returns `KERNEL_DENIED`. Spec 015 retired those endpoints and dropped the service to zero capabilities, so the property now held is strictly stronger than the one requested: the surface does not exist.

Recorded as supersession because the distinction matters to anyone auditing this later. The exploit path was closed twice, first by gating and then by deletion, and neither makes the other retrospectively wrong. The harness asserts the *absence* with five `it.each` cases, so a change reintroducing a write surface on that service fails there, which is exactly where the path would otherwise reopen.

## Scope

Sections 3.3 to 3.5 of spec 033 (compose topology, generated infra config, backend watch, restore marker) are pending and land next. The harness ships alone because it is what unblocks specs 026, 027, and the control plane, and it should not wait behind a compose topology nothing else depends on yet.

## Gate

title: feat(015): React-only frontend convergence; retire the hiq HTTP demo
body:
Phase 1c of the pivot (spec 001 §5.1).

Spec 001 §4.3 decided React-only on 2026-07-19 and left execution to "the follow-up frontend spec", which was never authored. The divergence then stood for ten days across three surfaces that disagreed with each other: the corpus said React-only, the tree carried both flavors, and `template.toml` defaulted to `vue`. That is exactly the drift the coupling gate exists to prevent, and it survived because the decision named no owner. Spec 015 is now that spec.

## The convergence

- `frontend-react/` becomes `frontend/`; the Vue source is deleted. Spec 015 takes the directory; **spec 006 keeps `backend/web/`**, the serving contract, which never knew what produced the bundle it serves. That independence is why this is a directory move rather than a rewrite.
- Package renamed `@enrahitu/frontend`.
- The cache-demo widget is deleted, which is what lets the `hiq` HTTP surface retire in the same change.

**The `frontend` slot is removed, not kept as a one-value knob.** Spec 001 §4.3 left that question open; the pivot closes it. enrahitu ships a working membership application rather than a shell to fill in, so the SPA carries the product's own screens and there is no framework choice left to offer. A slot with one allowed value is not a knob, it is a lie about where the variation lives. The extension seam is kinds and controllers (phase 4), not a choice of view library.

**Contract v0.7, and the version is where a caret pin actually sees the break.** Spec 009 §3.1 says removing a key is a "major" bump. The contract is at 0.x, where npm's caret makes the *minor* the breaking position: `^0.6.0` means `>=0.6.0 <0.7.0`, so 0.7.0 already breaks the pin. A literal 1.0.0 would additionally assert that this contract is stable, which is not a claim to make mid-pivot.

**`--frontend` fails loudly rather than becoming unknown.** `stamp.mjs` still matches the flag and raises a directed error naming the bump and the required pin. Dropping the case entirely would have produced "unknown argument: --frontend", which tells a factory operator nothing about why.

## The hiq demo retires

hiqlite is a library, not an API. Publishing the governed facade over HTTP added a second, weaker path to the same store and put six endpoints into the app model and the operator catalog that no feature used.

Retiring it *here* is deliberate: the SPA widget was its only consumer, so this is the moment the surface has no user, not merely the moment it has no justification.

`GET /hiq/health` survives (it returns a status string, leaks nothing, and is the probe the image smoke test curls). `backend/hiq/init.ts` and the kernel facade are untouched: those are the capability, the endpoints were the demo.

**The hiq service now holds zero capabilities**, and the five `demo:`-scoped capability definitions are deleted with them. This is the end of the spec 025 §3.1 exploit path, reached by subtraction rather than by constraint. Spec 025 found the service holding an unconstrained `cap.counter.add`, which let an unauthenticated caller forge the rate limiter's own `rl:` buckets and deny a chosen client its login; it closed that with a role gate plus a `demo:` keyPrefix narrowing. Both were correct, and both were mitigations of a service that still held write authority. It now has none. `health()` demands nothing, so nothing needs granting, and any endpoint added here later starts from an empty list.

## The coupling gate did its job

Seven paths changed whose owning specs this work touched without editing: `e2e.yml` (017), `verify.yml` (010), `app-manifest.json` and `app-model.json` (021), `ARCHITECTURE.md` (028), `docker-build.sh` (007), `spec-spine.toml` (000).

Each got a substantive amendment on its owning spec rather than a `Spec-Drift-Waiver`, because each is a real consequence rather than a mechanical refresh. The 007 amendment is worth calling out: the image worktree prune list got shorter, and the amendment restates *why* the prune exists (SPA source must never enter the image; only built bundles are carried in) so that removing a name from it is never mistaken for a size optimization.

## Gate

title: feat(032): the hiqlite interface contract, ten decisions before the addon
body:
Phase 1a of the pivot (spec 001 §5.1). The expanded hiqlite addon is the gate: nothing above it is testable until it exists, and its surface is either derived from stated requirements or guessed. This spec states the requirements, so phase 2 builds to a contract instead of to an intuition.

## The implementation check earned its keep

Every decision was verified against hiqlite's source rather than its documentation. Three checks changed the answer:

**The lock TTL is not configurable.** `const LOCK_VALID_SECONDS: i64 = 10` in `store/state_machine/memory/dlock_handler.rs`, with a `// TODO - lock_timeout` still sitting in `client/dlock.rs`. The intended answer to the lease decision was "TTL plus fencing token, tuned per controller". There is no tuning. Every lease expires in ten seconds whether or not the holder is finished, so any non-trivial reconcile **loses its lease while still running** and its replacement begins work concurrently. That is the normal case, not an edge case, which moves fencing from optional hardening to the thing that makes the lock usable at all.

**A fencing token already exists and is free.** The lock id is the raft `log_id` (`LockRequestPayload.log_id`), monotonically increasing across the cache raft group. Enforcement is a SQL predicate at the call site (`WHERE fence <= :token`), not addon machinery.

**`listen` is one global channel**, not per-topic, and its own doc comment warns that cache events may be replayed after a restart (hence `listen_after_start`). Filtering and idempotence are the consumer's job, which independently confirms the key-only envelope decision.

Two further constraints fell out: lock state lives in the non-durable cache raft group, and hiqlite's `Lock` releases on `Drop` asynchronously, which JavaScript has no deterministic equivalent for, so the addon must expose explicit `release()` with the finalizer as a backstop rather than the mechanism.

## The decisions that removed work

Four of the ten add nothing to the addon surface, which is the contract doing its job rather than failing to:

- **No CAS primitive.** `backend/kernel/decisions.ts` already implements it: a unique index on the parent pointer makes the insert itself the compare-and-swap. Inside a `txn` on a single-writer raft group that is exactly a CAS, and spec 024's three-attempt retry loop carries over with no change to its assertions.
- **No sequence generator.** Writes serialize through the leader, so `max(revision)+1` inside the transaction is already correct and lands in the same atomic unit as the row it stamps.
- **No migrate entry point.** Leader-only is a property of the store, not a feature to build; what remains is version comparison and idempotence, which is policy and belongs in application code where it is testable. Boot-time migration is refused because N replicas booting together would each attempt it.
- **No restore call.** Restore is a cluster reset, not a data restore.

## The audit placement conflict, resolved

The Decision chain needs linearizable read-modify-write on the head, which argues for hiqlite. Audit history is unbounded, which forbids hiqlite, since the full database replicates to every node. Both are true.

They are not actually in conflict: linearizability is needed only at the head, unboundedness is a property only of the tail. The head plus a hot window stay resident where CAS happens; sealed segments archive out, each linking to its predecessor's hash, so the chain verifies end to end without archived history being resident.

§3.9 keeps archive segments and hiqlite backups separate in a table, because conflating them fails a procurement review: a grant auditor asking for three-year-old board decisions is not served by a thirty-day operational snapshot schedule.

## `HQL_BACKUP_RESTORE` is designed out, not documented around

Left set in a container with a restart policy, it re-applies the backup on every restart and discards everything written since, turning a crash loop into silent repeated data loss. Restore routes through `docker/first-boot.mjs`, which writes a marker recording which backup was applied and refuses to re-apply. The operator sets the variable once; the platform makes it single-shot. That marker is phase 1b's work, which is why 1a and 1b are sequenced together.

## Resulting surface

Five new calls plus three backup calls. `query` / `queryConsistent` as distinct names rather than one flagged call, so the expensive choice is visible in review and the default is never silently wrong. `execute` / `txn`, where `txn` is required rather than optional because the resource-plus-outbox pair is the only atomic unit available (SQL writes and notify are in different raft groups and cannot be atomic under any API). `notify` / `listen` on a key-only envelope. `lock` returning a fencing token and an explicit release.

The accepted cost is stated rather than absorbed quietly: enabling `sqlite` pulls `rusqlite` and compiles SQLite-C into the `.node`, ending the addon's current no-bundled-SQLite-C property. It buys `backup = ["dep:cron", "s3", "sqlite"]` in the same change, and the app already runs SQLite through libSQL, so the process is consolidating onto one rather than gaining one.

## Gate

title: feat(001,002,010,030): pivot phase 0, realign the corpus to the product
body:
enrahitu becomes a **membership and association management platform** for non-profits and associations, shipped as a working application that organizations extend rather than fork.

Phase 0 is **specs only**: no runtime behavior changes. It exists so that no spec is left asserting something the pivot made false while later phases build against it, which is the failure mode where an approved spec makes every follow-up spec read as contradicting the corpus rather than extending it.

## Spec 001 (rewritten)

- **Names the product and the buyer.** A 200-member association has no ops team, and the organizations that could run a StatefulSet with PodDisruptionBudgets are not the ones buying association management. Every sizing and defaults question resolves against that reader.
- **Layer ownership with no overlap.** Encore.ts holds the edge and is not the process supervisor; hiqlite is the state layer, not a cache; rauthy is the principal authority, not a login page; application code holds intent and reconciliation.
- **N=1 is the primary mode**, not a degenerate case. Every spec states its behavior at N=1 first, because the reverse ordering is how a cluster assumption leaks into code paths a single container then works around.
- **Separates two invariants that were carried as one.** Deployment completeness survives and is the product. Zero-infrastructure *development* was wrong and is deleted. The rewrite record says why, so it is not re-proposed in six months: it is incompatible with a cluster-capable target (three-node raft cannot be developed where developers work), and it produced the dev/production divergence behind the spec 017 login failures that were visible only in CI.
- **4.7 dependency posture.** Turso benched (a driver swap, not a migration: `LedgerDriver` is a real interface and libSQL is 13 references). rauthy never forked: it has no embedding seam and forking is a permanent rebase tax against 75k lines under active development. Plus the three hiqlite properties that constrain every downstream spec: it replicates the full DB to every node so nothing unbounded may live in it; it runs two raft groups so SQL writes and notify **cannot be atomic together**; the cache group is not durable and is not backed up.
- **4.9 product scope bans.** No Slack, no card data, no MTA, no CMS, and the public surface is a new access path.
- **5.2 a disposition table for all 30 other specs**, so a contributor knows whether the spec they just opened is current, rewritten, or rewrite-pending.
- **5.3 the auth boundary**, decided rather than left open, because phase 1b's test harness needs a settled authentication story to authenticate against and a harness written for the wrong one gets rewritten.

## Spec 002 (surgical)

Deletes two false prohibitions ("hiqlite runs single-node", "clustering is out of scope for v0") and the dlock/notify deferral whose condition is now met.

Deliberately adds nothing. The spec is `implementation: complete`, and a complete spec that describes an unbuilt surface is a claim the coupling gate cannot catch. Deleting a false invariant and describing an unbuilt target are different operations; only the first belongs in phase 0.

## Spec 030 (rewritten)

The first version accepted the premise that the single container was a limitation and designed an escape: stateless app containers, a singleton IdP, a shared external ledger. That forced a role selector, a key-injection ceremony, and a shared store into existence. All three were consequences of treating hiqlite as a cache and rauthy as a singleton, and clustering rauthy's own hiqlite dissolves all three.

What replaces them: one uniform topology at two sizes, the StatefulSet placement requirements, and the three operational rules that turn a routine node drain into an outage if omitted (PodDisruptionBudget `maxUnavailable: 1`; readiness reflects quorum but liveness must not, or a transient quorum loss becomes a permanent restart loop; anti-affinity). Section 6 records what was deleted and why.

## The AGPL boundary guard

The pivot brief asserted `scripts/check-licenses.mjs` already failed the build loudly. **It did not exist in this repo**, and `governance-native` appeared nowhere in the tree, so the invariant was unenforced exactly where such a dependency would be declared.

Three independent checks, because each catches a different mistake: declared dependencies (the edit, pre-install), the committed lockfile's recorded licenses (the transitive pull), and the installed tree (a lockfile that lies). 8 tests exercising the failure paths, including a forbidden package claiming a permissive license, since the whole hazard is that the two `@statecrafting` names differ by one word.

Two placement decisions: it runs in **this** repo because this repo's `package.json` is where the dependency would be declared, and a guard living only upstream does not gate these PRs; and it runs **before** the build, because its job is to refuse a dependency graph and the cheapest moment to learn the graph is wrong is before anything compiles against it.

## Gate

compile 32 specs / 0 warnings, index 32 mappings / 0 diagnostics, lint 0/0/0, index fresh, couple OK on 9 paths, typecheck clean, 151 tests across 18 files.

`check:model` needs no rerun: the app model does not embed the `package.json` field this PR changes, which matters because `build:app` corrupts `node_modules/encore.dev` and does not self-restore.

title: feat(025): harden the exposed surface; author specs 025-031
body:
An external evaluation of the packaged image found four defects that exist only once the cell is reachable by a stranger, plus a set of product gaps around operating one over time. All four were verified against the code before being acted on, and two were worse than reported.

## The defects

**`clientIp` preferred forged `X-Forwarded-For` over the socket address it already held** (`backend/auth/http.ts`). The report flagged only the rate limiter; the real blast radius is wider. The auth-tier limiter was independently bypassable, and the two defects compose: an attacker poisons a victim's bucket while staying unlimited themselves. Replaced by `backend/lib/client-identity.ts` with hop-counted XFF trust.

**The six `/hiq/*` endpoints shipped `expose: true` with no `auth: true`.** Correct while the surface was a developer's laptop, wrong once the packaged image binds `0.0.0.0:8080`: it published unauthenticated writes into the raft-replicated store, and because the service also held an unconstrained `cap.counter.add`, it published the rate limiter's own counters. Now operator-gated, with grants narrowed to a `demo:` prefix. `GET /hiq/health` stays public: it returns a status string and is the probe the image smoke curls.

**Liveness and readiness were one endpoint.** Split into `/healthz` (touches no dependency) and `/readyz` (checks the ledger), with a `HEALTHCHECK` on the former. A transient ledger blip must not restart the container, because the die-together supervisor would take rauthy down with it.

**`/metrics` was unauthenticated.** Now behind a bearer token provisioned at first boot, so the packaged image authenticates by default; an explicitly supplied value wins, letting a fleet inject one shared token.

## A design correction the extraction gate caught

This spec originally called for mounting `apiRateLimit` on the `hiq` service. `enrahitu-extract` refused the model, correctly: middleware runs under the mounting service's kernel attribution, so the limiter's own `rl:`-prefixed counter writes would have been adjudicated as `hiq`, denied against the new `demo:`-scoped grants, and swallowed by `increment()`'s fail-open path. The limiter would have enforced nothing while appearing to. Widening the grant would have reopened the exploit, so the answer was the admin service's no-limiter precedent. The spec was amended before the code, not after.

## Also in this branch

Specs 026 through 031 authored as pending work orders: IdP mail delivery, operational verbs, operator documentation, supply-chain provenance, infra topology, and admin evidence export. Spec 001 section 4.1 gains the thesis clarification that completeness, not isolation, is the invariant. The spec 025 amendments are recorded in the six owning specs (002, 004, 005, 007, 021, 022) rather than only in 025.

## Status

Spec 025 is `implementation: in-progress`, deliberately. Behavior is complete and the gate is green, but four acceptance items need endpoint-level proof against a running gateway, and this repo has no app-level test harness: every existing test is either a pure module or a subprocess. Section 5 records exactly what remains. That harness is phase 1b of the follow-up work.

Gate: typecheck clean, 143 tests across 17 files, compile/index/lint/index-check green, couple OK on 31 paths.

title: test(007): harden the entrypoint harness against slow runners
body:
Mirrors the same fix on the statecraft side (statecrafting/statecraft#70), so the two copies of this test stay byte-identical apart from the spec reference in the header comment. Both came out of the automated review of #70, and both are about the harness, not the handler.

**Readiness poll ceiling.** The poll allowed 100 × 20ms = 2s before delivering the signal. On a slow runner the signal could land before the traps were installed, which fails as exit 143 and reads like a broken handler rather than a slow start: the worst kind of flake, one that accuses the code under test. The budget is now 10s against the 15s test timeout, and exhausting it throws as itself rather than signalling into the dark.

**Empty argument to `wait -n`.** With `startApp: false` the harness expanded `${APP_PID:-}` into an empty argument. It was masked by `set +e` and discarded stderr, so it never failed anything, but it was sloppy. The wait list is now built to match the stubs that actually exist.

No change to `docker/entrypoint.sh`. Test passes 4/4, `tsc --noEmit` clean.

Spec-Drift-Waiver: test-quality only. This changes `docker/entrypoint.test.ts` and nothing else: no behavior, no interface, and no design decision moves, so spec 007's 2026-07-25 amendment already describes what this test covers, exactly and unchanged. Amending the spec here would mean editing an owning spec purely to satisfy a mechanical refresh, which `.claude/rules/adversarial-prompt-refusal.md` names as the thing to waive rather than do.

title: fix(007): forward container stop to rauthy and the app
body:
## The defect

`docker/entrypoint.sh` is PID 1 in the shipped image, so the runtime delivers SIGTERM to it and to nothing else. With no trap installed, bash's default action ended the shell alone and left rauthy and the app running until the grace period expired and they were SIGKILLed. The `kill` on the die-together path only ever ran when a supervised process exited on its own.

rauthy is what pays for this. Its embedded hiqlite holds lock files for the WAL and the state machine, and a SIGKILL never releases them, so **every** boot after **every** ordinary restart began unclean. Observed on the live statecraft control plane 2026-07-25, on a boot with nothing else wrong with it:

```
WARN hiqlite_wal::log_store: LockFile /data/rauthy/db/logs exists already - this is not a clean start!
WARN hiqlite::store::state_machine::sqlite::state_machine: Lock file already exists: /data/rauthy/db/state_machine/lock
WARN hiqlite_wal::log_store: LockFile /data/rauthy/db/logs_cache exists already - this is not a clean start!
```

The warning is not the whole cost. On that same restart it escalated three times before a boot got through:

```
thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked at hiqlite-wal-0.14.0/src/log_store.rs:47:21:
LockFile /data/rauthy/db/logs is locked and in use by another process
```

which aborts rauthy, which die-together turns into a container exit, which the restart policy turns into a crash loop. Three restarts and roughly forty-five seconds of extra downtime on a routine pod replacement, with no bound on how many it could have been.

## The fix

A stop handler that forwards SIGTERM/SIGINT to both children and waits for them before exiting 0 (the container was asked to stop and did). Armed immediately after `RAUTHY_PID` is assigned, so a stop during the rauthy health wait is covered too, and tolerant of an unset `APP_PID` in that window.

## Tests

`docker/entrypoint.test.ts` covers the **shipped** function rather than a copy of it: it lifts the `shutdown()` body out of `docker/entrypoint.sh` by text and runs it against stub children, so editing the real function is what breaks the test. Four cases: both traps installed, SIGTERM and SIGINT each reaching rauthy and the app, and a signal arriving before the app has started.

Verified in the other direction by hand, because it is the whole argument for the change: with the trap removed the harness exits 143 and neither child is signalled at all.

One wrinkle worth knowing for anyone extending this: the stubs run `sleep 30 & wait $!` rather than a plain `sleep 30`, because bash defers a trap until the running foreground command returns. A foreground-sleeping stub swallows the signal for 30 seconds and proves nothing. That cost me a first draft.

This is the first test in the repo over `docker/`, which is the point: the entrypoint is a shell script that has now caused two production incidents, and "PID 1 forwards its signals" is not reachable from a TypeScript test.

## Verification

14 test files / 109 passed, `tsc --noEmit` clean, `spec-spine lint` 0/0/0, `couple` OK across 3 paths.

## Note for consumers

Stamped apps carry their own copy of the entrypoint (statecraft's diverges by four hunks, recorded in its spec 002), so the same handler has to land in each of them. It does not arrive via a pin. The statecraft-side copy is going up separately.

title: feat(007,016): non-root image (USER node) + admin deps in image.yml
body:
## Summary

Chassis queue item D3 (from the 2026-07-23 statecraft handoff), plus the pre-existing main breakage its validation dispatch surfaced.

- **Non-root image** (spec 007 amendment): the final image sets `USER node` (uid/gid 1000) and owns `/data` at build time so a fresh named volume inherits writable ownership. This is the chassis half of the statecraft finding: the fleet already runs the pod as uid 1000 with `fsGroup: 1000` (statecraft spec 006, E2E finding 3), and statecraft spec 009 records that hardening the image UID is an enrahitu chassis change, not something to improvise in a Deployment. Nothing in the container needs root: every runtime write lives under `/data` (rauthy's `data_dir` included; verified against `first-boot.mjs`'s write targets) and both listeners are unprivileged ports. Migration is stated honestly in the amendment: Kubernetes heals legacy root-owned volumes via `fsGroup` on mount; plain docker needs a one-time `chown -R 1000:1000`, with `--user 0` as the escape hatch.
- **image.yml installs the admin bundle's deps** (spec 016 amendment): `frontend-admin` (spec 023, PR #27) patched `verify.yml` and `e2e.yml` but missed the image workflow, so `docker-build.sh`'s `build:web-admin` died on missing packages: main has been silently image-broken since that merge, unnoticed because `image.yml` runs on cron/dispatch only (the exact failure mode spec 007's 2026-07-22 amendment records). title: fix(004,005): RP-initiated logout ends the rauthy session
body:
## Summary

Chassis queue item D1 (from the 2026-07-23 statecraft handoff): app sign-out revoked the app session but never told rauthy, so rauthy's own session cookie survived and the next login silently re-authenticated without credentials. Fixed with OIDC RP-initiated logout, same-origin like the rest of spec 005, with the design fork resolved in the owning specs before code.

- **The hint rides the browser, not the store** (spec 005 amendment): the rauthy callback keeps `tokens.id_token` in an `oidc_id_hint` cookie: httpOnly, path-scoped to `/api/v1/auth`, refresh-session lifetime. The rejected alternative (a column on the refresh-token row) is recorded with its reasons: the refresh-token store is hash-only by design, rotation would need carry plumbing, and the hint is only ever needed by the browser's own logout round-trip.
- **Logout returns the end-session URL** (spec 004 amendment): with a hint present and the driver configured, `POST /api/v1/auth/logout` answers `redirectUrl` = same-origin `<issuer>oidc/logout?id_token_hint=...&post_logout_redirect_uri=<frontend root>`; otherwise the frontend root, so the mock driver's behavior is byte-identical. `clearAuthCookies` clears the hint alongside the auth cookies with the matching path.
- **Both SPAs follow `redirectUrl`** (spec 006/015 amendments) with a document navigation; the react flavor's logout action drops its client-side `redirect("/")`, which cannot reach a URL outside the SPA route table.
- **Registration already existed**: both client bootstraps have carried `post_logout_redirect_uris` since spec 007's first boot; the dev bootstrap now also registers the Vite origin (`http://localhost:5173/`) so hot-dev round-trips are legal.

title: feat(024): decision-chain integrity: CAS append, fatal forks, signing
body:
## Summary

Spec 024 (decision-chain integrity) plus the ledger-durability law amendments it was evaluated with, from the 2026-07-23 statecraft handoff.

- **CAS append at the store** (spec 024 §3.1): a unique parent index on `kernel_decisions.prev_hash` plus a transactional head read make every append a compare-and-swap on the chain head, both dialects. A lost race reloads the head and re-chains (three attempts), then fails loud with a typed `LedgerIntegrityError`. The in-process queue stays as concurrency discipline; it is no longer the chain's only ordering authority, so a second writer (deploy overlap, accidental replica) can no longer fork the chain silently.
- **Fatal verification at init** (§3.2): init runs the full `verifyChain` pass (plus signatures); an integrity failure on the init path is process-fatal, extending spec 021 §3.4's fail-closed doctrine to the ledger. Under vitest the same error rejects instead, so the path is provable in-process.
- **Marked denial-append loss** (§3.3): denial appends stay fire-and-forget (spec 021 §3.6 policy kept); a durable dirty flag in `kernel_ledger_meta` brackets in-flight appends, and an unclean end of a bracket ledgers one crash-window marker Decision (outcome `unknown`) at the next boot. The residual unmarked window is one durable write wide and documented.
- **Signing activated** (§3.4): the `ledger.signing` policy the model has declared since spec 021 goes live consumer-side: detached ed25519 over `record_hash` in a sibling `signature` column (native record shape and verifier untouched), keyed by `ENRAHITU_LEDGER_SIGNING_KEY` (64-char hex seed), dormant when unset, fail-loud when malformed, verified as a chain-suffix property.
- **Spec 001 amendment**: three constraints enter the thesis as law: the outbox rule (no invariant spans hiqlite and CoreLedger without an outbox and idempotent replay), the Phase B doctrine that the chain head moves into hiqlite Raft when cells cluster (the self-hosted analogue of Fluree's commits-durable/indexes-reproducible split; nothing built until hiqlite stops being per-process), and the portability boundary (the decorator API stays driver-portable for application tables; the Decision chain and future fact models live on the raw-driver layer and may pin a driver family).
- **Spec 007 amendment + entrypoint**: `ENRAHITU_REQUIRED_ENV`, a fleet-declared pre-flight list of env names that must be set and non-empty before anything starts; all missing names report together, one failure. Reduces statecraft's Deployment-command stopgap (statecraft PR #64) to setting one variable.

Sibling-territory coupling follows the spec 011 pattern: `backend/kernel/decisions.ts` stays owned by spec 021, whose amendment records the four §3.6 facts that moved; spec 024 establishes the new test file.

## Testing

- `spec-spine compile` (25 specs) / `lint --fail-on-warn` / `index check` / `couple --base origin/main --head HEAD` (7 paths, no drift): all clean
- `npm run typecheck`: clean
